title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Move combinational MUL/DIV out of EX into a stalling multi-cycle muldiv unit
motivation:
Baseline Fmax is 5.44 MHz: the worst path is 199.8 ns / 150 logic levels
(mem_wb.rd -> forward_unit -> ex_stage operand mux -> alu -> EX/MEM / dmem
address). Those 150 levels are the 32-bit combinational `/` and `%` in
alu.sv (plus three separate 64-bit multiplies mul_ss / mul_uu / mul_su
that all hang off the same forwarded operands). Every other path in the
5-stage pipe (fwd compare + mux + 32-bit add/compare + pc mux, load-align,
decode) is an order of magnitude shorter, so the circuit is limited
purely by one rarely-used unit. CoreMark's timed region contains
essentially zero DIV/REM (only ~3k MULs per iteration out of ~449k
cycles), so making DIV/MUL multi-cycle costs ~1% cycles while the clock
can run several times faster. fitness = iter/cycle x Fmax, so this is
almost entirely an Fmax win.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Take ALU_MUL..ALU_REMU out of the combinational ALU and execute them in a
new registered, multi-cycle `muldiv` unit that holds the instruction in EX
(pipeline-stalling it) until a registered `done` flag is set. Nothing
deeper than ~one 33-bit add/sub or one DSP multiply stage remains between
any two flops.

1. New rtl/muldiv.sv (ports: clock, reset, start, op[4:0], a, b,
   consume; outputs: done (flop), result). FSM IDLE -> work -> DONE.
   * Capture cycle (start = md_op && IDLE && !done && !stall_ex_mem):
     latch the already-forwarded rs1/rs2 (a_q/b_q) and op_q. Starting only
     when EX/MEM is not dmem-stalled guarantees the operands are the same
     forwarded values the baseline would have captured on its commit
     cycle. Latching is mandatory: the forwarding sources move on while
     EX is stalled, and ID/EX.rs?_val is a stale regfile read.
   * MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU: ONE shared signed 33x33 multiplier instead of
     the three 64-bit products now in alu.sv. mul_a = {a_signed&a[31], a},
     mul_b = {b_signed&b[31], b} where a_signed = (op != MULHU) and
     b_signed = (op is MUL/MULH). Cycle 1: prod <= mul_a * mul_b (66-bit
     register, so the DSP path is reg -> DSP -> reg and Gowin can absorb
     the input/output regs). Cycle 2: done=1, result = hi ? prod[63:32] :
     prod[31:0] (hi is a registered flag; only a 2:1 mux after flops).
     => 2 stall cycles per MUL.
   * DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU: radix-2 restoring divider, 32 iterations of
     {rem,quo} <<= 1; if (rem >= div) rem -= div, quo[0] = 1 (one 33-bit
     compare/sub per cycle). A PREP cycle takes |a|, |b| from the latched
     registers (negate-in-register, never on the forwarding path), a FIX
     cycle conditionally negates quo (signs differ) / rem (a negative).
     RV32M corner cases: b==0 -> DIV/DIVU quotient = 0xFFFFFFFF and REM/
     REMU = original a (suppress the sign-fix negate of the quotient when
     b==0, otherwise a negative dividend would yield +1 instead of -1);
     INT_MIN / -1 falls out of the unsigned algorithm correctly
     (quo = 0x80000000, rem = 0). ~35 cycles, which is irrelevant since
     the timed region has ~0 divisions. `done` stays high until consumed.

2. rtl/ex_stage.sv: md_op = in.valid && in.ctrl.alu_op >= ALU_MUL (tied to
   0 under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`, where the existing combinational
   (a+b)^const stand-ins in alu.sv remain in force and no stall ever
   occurs). Instantiate muldiv fed by the post-forward rs1 / alu_b (rs2)
   values; consume = md_op && done && !stall. Export
   md_stall = md_op && !done. EX/MEM register next-state priority:
   reset -> hold on `stall` (dmem) -> on md_stall write a bubble
   (valid=0, ctrl=0, reg_write=0 so forwarding sees nothing) -> normal.
   On the normal path alu_result <= is_jump ? pc+4 : md_op ? md_result :
   alu_result. For RVFI, rs1_val/rs2_val written into EX/MEM must be the
   unit's latched a_q/b_q when md_op && done (the live forward muxes may be
   stale by then); those fields are RVFI-only and pruned from the timed
   netlist.

3. rtl/hazard_unit.sv + rtl/core.sv: new input md_stall. stall_if |=
   md_stall, stall_id |= md_stall (ID/EX holds, PC holds; the younger
   instruction is simply re-fetched/held exactly as for a dmem stall),
   flush_id additionally masked with !md_stall, hold_mem_wb unchanged
   (MEM/WB keeps advancing so the older in-flight instructions retire and
   the EX/MEM bubble flows through). dmem_stall still has priority over
   everything: while EX/MEM is held for the dmem bus the muldiv engine may
   keep running and `done` simply waits until !stall_ex_mem. md_stall is
   a function of flops only (id_ex.alu_op decode + done), so it adds no
   deep logic to the stall/redirect fan-out.

4. rtl/alu.sv: in the non-ALTOPS branch drop the MUL/DIV/REM arms and the
   three 64-bit products (op default = 0); keep the ALTOPS branch exactly
   as is. This deletes the 150-level divider and ~6 DSPs' worth of
   duplicated multipliers from the EX timing path and shrinks LUT area.
   Cocotb: test_alu.py keeps the base-ISA vectors and the ALTOPS-mode
   expectations only; new test_muldiv.py drives the unit (start, wait for
   done, check result) with all the existing exact-bit MUL/MULH/MULHU/
   MULHSU/DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vectors plus corner cases (x/0, INT_MIN/-1,
   random signed/unsigned sweeps vs a Python reference, back-to-back
   ops, start during a held `consume`). test_pipeline.py's source list
   must include muldiv.sv.

Expected outcome: remaining critical paths are fwd-mux -> 32-bit add /
compare -> pc mux / BSRAM address and DSP reg->reg, i.e. roughly 15-20 ns,
versus 199.8 ns today, with CoreMark cycles up by ~1-2% (two stall cycles
on each of ~3k multiplies per iteration). Note the replacement multiplier
can be re-pipelined a further stage if the DSP path becomes the worst
path after P&R.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r1s0 (improvement, +811.96%): Fmax was set by one rarely-executed unit (the combinational 32-bit `/` and `%` in alu.sv, ~150 logic levels, 199.8 ns), so moving MUL/DIV/REM into a registered multi-cycle `muldiv` that stalls EX raised fitness ~9x for ~1% extra cycles, since CoreMark's timed region has ~0 DIVs and few MULs; when the critical path runs through an op CoreMark seldom issues, multi-cycle it with a stall (hold EX, bubble into EX/MEM, latch forwarded operands) before tuning common-case paths.

title: Pull MUL/DIV out of the EX combinational path into a multi-cycle muldiv unit
motivation:
Baseline Fmax is 5.44 MHz (worst path 199.8 ns, 156 cells:
forward_unit -> ex_stage -> alu -> ex_stage). That path is the ALU's
combinational 32x32 multipliers and the 32-bit `/` and `%` operators. alu.sv
instantiates three 64-bit multipliers (ss, uu, su) plus signed and unsigned
divide/remainder in one always_comb, and every EX result goes through the
output mux behind them. The same logic is the main reason the design is
12.3k LUT4 against a 10k target. Every other path in this 5-stage in-order
core (forwarding mux -> add/shift/compare -> redirect -> PC mux, regfile
read, load alignment) should be around 20 ns or less. So removing the
mul/div cone from EX should raise Fmax several-fold. Baseline CoreMark is
about 2.23 CoreMark/MHz, and MUL/DIV are a small share of the dynamic
instruction mix, so taking a few stall cycles on them costs little IPC
compared with the Fmax gain.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make multiply and divide multi-cycle. A new rtl/muldiv.sv replaces the
combinational `*`, `/` and `%` in the EX critical cone. The EX stage stalls
the front of the pipeline while a MUL/DIV is in flight.

1. rtl/muldiv.sv (new). It has a small FSM: IDLE -> (MUL1 -> MUL2) or
   (PREP -> 32 x ITER -> FIX) -> DONE. Inputs are the post-forward
   rs1/rs2, the alu_op and a `valid` signal. Outputs are `md_stall`
   (= the op is a MUL/DIV in EX and state != DONE), `result[31:0]`, and
   the captured operands `a_q` and `b_q`.
   - The unit captures the forwarded operands in the first EX cycle.
     The forwarding sources disappear once a bubble enters EX/MEM, so
     later phases and the RVFI rs1/rs2 values use only a_q/b_q.
   - Multiply: the 33-bit operand is split into a 17-bit signed hi half
     ({sign_ext_bit, x[31:16]}) and a 16-bit unsigned lo half. The four
     17x17 signed partial products (ll, lh, hl, hh) are registered at the
     end of the first cycle. Gowin should map them to MULT18X18 DSPs, and
     a 17x17 LUT multiplier is also short. The next cycle adds
     ll + ((lh+hl)<<16) + (hh<<32) into a registered 64-bit result, and
     the cycle after that is DONE. That is 2 stall cycles per MUL/MULH*.
     MUL takes result[31:0]; MULH/MULHSU/MULHU take result[63:32]. Signed
     and unsigned flavours differ only in the extension bit of the 33-bit
     operands: sa = signed_a & a[31], sb = signed_b & b[31].
   - Divide/remainder: radix-2 restoring divider, one bit per cycle,
     about 35 cycles per op. PREP takes absolute values for DIV/REM.
     ITER does shift/compare/subtract on a 32-bit remainder and
     quotient. FIX applies the sign fix-up. The RV32M special cases are
     handled explicitly: div by 0 gives quotient all-ones and remainder
     = dividend, and INT_MIN/-1 gives quotient INT_MIN and remainder 0.
     Division is rare in CoreMark (compilers turn constant divides into
     multiplies), so the long latency is acceptable.

2. rtl/alu.sv: add `parameter ENABLE_MD = 1`. With ENABLE_MD=1 the module
   behaves exactly as today, so test_alu.py (exact bit results for every
   M op) keeps passing unchanged. With ENABLE_MD=0 a generate-if drops all
   the multiply/divide expressions, and ALU_MUL..ALU_REMU fall into the
   default arm. The RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS branch stays byte-for-byte as is,
   and formal builds still use the combinational XOR stand-ins.

3. rtl/ex_stage.sv:
   - Instantiate alu with ENABLE_MD=0 for non-ALTOPS builds. Under
     `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS keep ENABLE_MD=1 and tie md_stall to 0, so
     formal sees no multi-cycle behaviour.
   - Instantiate muldiv and select the EX result:
     `ex_result = md_op ? md_result : alu_result`. This is a 2:1 mux on
     the existing alu_result -> EX/MEM path.
   - Add output `md_stall`. When md_stall is high and the dmem `stall`
     is low, the EX/MEM register captures a bubble (`reg_q <= '0`), so
     valid=0 and the control bits are zero.
   - dmem `stall` keeps priority and still holds EX/MEM.
   - In the DONE cycle with no dmem stall the instruction moves into
     EX/MEM and the FSM returns to IDLE. In DONE with a dmem stall the
     FSM stays in DONE, because ID/EX is held too.
   - reg_q.rs1_val and rs2_val take a_q/b_q when the op is MUL/DIV.
     They feed only RVFI, so they add no timed logic.
   - Branches and jumps are never MUL/DIV, so `redirect` can never
     coincide with md_stall.

4. rtl/hazard_unit.sv and rtl/core.sv: add an `md_stall` input and wire it
   from ex_stage. `stall_if |= md_stall` and `stall_id |= md_stall`. The
   PC and ID/EX hold, and the same instruction is re-fetched from the same
   pc when the stall releases, as already happens for load-use. flush_id
   and flush_if are unchanged. load_use_hazard cannot fire during an md
   stall because the instruction in ID/EX is not a load. hold_mem_wb is
   still only dmem_stall: the older instruction in EX/MEM drains to MEM/WB
   normally on the first stall cycle, and bubbles follow it.
   rvfi_order increments only on mem_wb.valid, so retirement order stays
   strictly +1.

5. test/test_pipeline.py: add "muldiv.sv" to the explicit source list.
   Add test/test_muldiv.py with directed vectors for every M op,
   including the div-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 corner cases and
   back-to-back MUL -> dependent-instruction forwarding. Also check MUL
   directly behind a load that is dmem-stalled.

After the change the ALU cone is add/sub/shift/compare only. I expect the
critical path to be forwarding -> ALU/branch compare -> redirect or PC mux,
at roughly 15-30 ns, so Fmax of about 30-60 MHz. LUT count should fall
substantially, since the three 64-bit multipliers and the four dividers
are gone. DSP use is 4 MULT18X18, which are free resources. The IPC cost
is 2 stall cycles per MUL and about 35 per DIV/REM, expected under 10% of
cycles on CoreMark. Net fitness should rise several-fold, far above the
4.6% acceptance threshold.

title: Zero-bubble fetch-time predecode predictor (JAL + BTFN + 4-entry RAS) verified in EX
motivation:
The baseline resolves every taken branch and every JAL/JALR in EX and pays a
one-slot redirect bubble each time (flush_if + flush_id, pc <= redirect_target).
Because ~22% of fetch slots are already lost to imem stalls, each wasted
fetch slot costs ~1/0.78 = 1.28 cycles. On CoreMark (4.49M cycles / 10 iters,
~14% of dynamic instructions are taken branches or jumps: loop back-edges,
calls, returns) this redirect tax is on the order of 10-12% of all cycles.
Fmax is pinned at ~5.4 MHz by the combinational mul/div ALU path (199 ns, 156
logic cells), so every other path in the core has >150 ns of slack. Predictor
logic placed in the fetch/EX-redirect paths (a few LUT levels) is therefore
free in Fmax terms and the whole gain shows up as iterations/cycle.
The bench imem is combinational from imem_addr = pc register (cosim and FPGA
wrapper both), and if_stage already uses imem_data combinationally in the same
cycle as pc, so the fetched instruction can be pre-decoded in IF and used to
choose the NEXT pc at the same clock edge: zero-bubble prediction without a
BTB, tags, or any table that needs update/aging logic.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a stateless-plus-tiny-RAS predictor to if_stage and turn the EX redirect
into a mispredict check.

IF-stage predecode (on out.instr = imem_data, only when out.valid && !stall,
i.e. the fetch is real and pc is actually advancing this edge):
  * JAL (opcode 1101111): predict taken, target = pc + J-imm.
  * BRANCH (opcode 1100011) with instr[31]==1 (backward): predict taken (BTFN),
    target = pc + B-imm. Forward branches predict not-taken (pc+4).
  * "ret" pattern JALR (opcode 1100111, funct3 0, rd==x0, rs1 in {x1,x5}) and
    RAS non-empty: predict taken, target = RAS top, pop.
  * JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5} (call): push pc+4 onto a 4-entry RAS (shift
    register of 32-bit entries + 3-bit depth, saturating; overwrite-oldest on
    overflow; reset clears depth only).
  * Only predict a JAL/branch taken if target bit 1 is zero (instr[21]==0 for
    J, instr[8]==0 for B) so pc never becomes misaligned.
next_pc priority: redirect (EX) > predicted target > pc+4. imem_addr stays a
plain register output of pc (no comb path from imem_data to imem_addr, which
the cosim harness's once-per-cycle imem sampling requires).
The per-instruction predicted next-pc `pred_next` (= predicted target if taken
else pc+4) is added to if_id_t and id_ex_t (core_pkg.sv) and latched in the
ID/EX register in id_stage.sv. Capture and pc-advance happen on exactly the
same edges (both gated by !stall; redirect/imem-stall bubbles carry
valid=0), so pred_next always names the pc that follows this instruction in
the fetch stream. Only correct-path instructions are ever predecoded, because
the single wrong-path fetch slot is flushed (valid=0) in the same cycle EX
detects the mispredict; hence RAS push/pop is never polluted by wrong-path
instructions.

EX-stage verification (ex_stage.sv): compute actual_next exactly as the
existing pc_next expression (misalign_fault ? pc+4 : is_jump ? jump_target :
branch_taken ? branch_target : pc+4). Then
    redirect        = in.valid && (actual_next != in.pred_next)
    redirect_target = actual_next
This replaces `(branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault`. It covers every
case uniformly: correct predicted-taken (no redirect, zero bubble), correct
predicted-not-taken (no redirect), taken-but-predicted-not (redirect, 1 bubble
= today's cost), predicted-taken-but-not-taken / non-branch alias / misaligned
trap (redirect to pc+4), JALR target mismatch (redirect). RVFI pc_next/pc_wdata
keep using actual_next, so the riscv-formal pc_fwd/unique/liveness/ill checks
see unchanged architectural behavior; mispredicts are architecturally
invisible. hazard_unit/forward_unit/core.sv interfaces are unchanged (redirect
and redirect_target keep their meaning), and the existing "redirect overrides
stall" and dmem-stall-hold behavior is preserved because the mispredict
compare is idempotent while the instruction is held in ID/EX.

Expected effect: JAL (100%), most JALR returns (RAS), and loop back-edges
(~85-90% taken) no longer cost a bubble; only forward-taken branches, loop
exits, data-dependent branches and indirect non-ret jumps still pay 1 slot.
Estimated ~60-70% of redirects removed => ~0.11-0.13 cycles/instr saved out of
~1.5-1.8 => 6-8% fewer cycles per CoreMark iteration, with Fmax unchanged
(new paths: imem_data->predecode->adder->pc mux ~15-20 ns; fwd->jalr adder->
32b compare->redirect ~40 ns, both far below 199 ns). If the RAS proves
troublesome in implementation it can be dropped (JAL+BTFN alone is still
~4-6%), but it is a small shift-register block and returns are ~3% of
CoreMark's dynamic instruction mix.

changes.description: Add `logic [31:0] pred_next` to if_id_t and id_ex_t (predicted next-pc of the fetched instruction). ex_mem_t/mem_wb_t unchanged.

Add predecode of imem_data (JAL, backward BRANCH, ret-JALR via RAS), 4-entry x 32-bit RAS shift stack with depth counter (push on call rd in {x1,x5}, pop on ret; updated only when out.valid && !stall && !reset), pc update priority redirect > predicted target > pc+4, drive out.pred_next. imem_addr remains the pc register.
Latch in.pred_next into the ID/EX register (reg_q.pred_next) alongside pc/instr/valid; zero on reset/flush as with other fields.

Replace redirect/redirect_target with a mispredict check: actual_next (same expression as reg_q.pc_next) compared against in.pred_next, gated by in.valid; redirect_target = actual_next. Keep reg_q.pc_next/RVFI path unchanged.

title: Take EX redirect off the IF->ID NOP mux / load-use / regfile-address path
motivation:
Gowin timing on the current champion (place option 0: 49.67 MHz, worst path
25.43 ns arrival incl. 5.3 ns clock insertion) shows the critical path is
regfile BSRAM out -> EX forward mux (4 LUTs) -> 32-bit branch compare carry
chain -> `redirect` -> if_stage's `(flush || redirect) ? NOP : imem_data`
instruction mux (rs2_addr_w_2_s1, fanout 8) -> hazard_unit's load-use
comparator (u_hazard n12..n14 carry chain) -> stall_id/flush_id -> ID/EX
register enables (fanout 33) -> D. All 25 reported worst paths (ending at
id_ex rs?_val, pc, reg_q.valid/ctrl) share this chain: roughly the last
10.6 ns of a 20 ns path is spent AFTER the branch compare, going back
through decode-side logic that does not need to know about the redirect.
The NOP substitution on `redirect` is redundant: a redirect can only come
from a branch/jump in EX, which is never a load, so load_use_hazard is
already 0 whenever redirect=1; the wrong-path instruction in ID is already
killed by flush_id (ID/EX captures '0 on redirect) while PC is overridden by
redirect_target.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the IF/ID combinational payload depend only on early signals: in
if_stage.sv use `out.instr = flush ? NOP : imem_data` and
`out.valid = !flush` (drop `|| redirect` from both), and in hazard_unit.sv
set `flush_if = imem_stall` (no `redirect`). Everything else stays: PC
next-state still gives redirect priority over stall; flush_id still includes
redirect (so ID/EX captures '0 on a taken branch/jump unless held by
dmem_stall/md_stall); stall_if/stall_id/stall_ex_mem/hold_mem_wb unchanged.
Branch resolution then terminates at the PC mux and the ID/EX synchronous
clear instead of continuing through the instr mux, load-use comparator and
stall enables, removing ~8 logic levels / ~10 ns from the worst path.
Correctness argument: (1) with redirect asserted EX holds a branch/jump, so
id_ex.mem_read=0 and load_use_hazard=0 — the NOP no longer needs to hide a
spurious load-use; (2) the wrong-path instruction decoded in ID this cycle is
zeroed by flush_id; if dmem_stall/md_stall instead holds ID/EX nothing is
captured and PC is still overridden by redirect, and the branch re-asserts
redirect next cycle exactly as before; (3) rvfi_valid only ever comes from
MEM/WB, so a wrong-path instruction can never retire; (4) imem_stall still
forces the NOP, so a not-ready fetch is still a bubble. IPC is bit-for-bit
unchanged (no cycle-level behaviour changes). Empirically verified in a
scratch run of `make timing TARGET=bench` with exactly these three-line
edits: place option 0 Fmax 49.67 -> 58.66 MHz (+18%), LUT4 2446 -> 2466, FF
unchanged. The new worst path (22.3 ns) is the textbook regfile -> forward
mux -> ALU adder -> dmem address path, so no further gain is expected from
this change alone.

title: Cut the EX redirect out of the IF->ID instruction/regfile-address loop; precompute branch/JAL target in ID
motivation:
After the muldiv fix the 25.4 ns worst paths (log.jsonl hyp-001-r1s0 and
hyp-002-r1s1) both run clock_ibuf > u_id (ID/EX flops) > u_ex > u_if >
u_hazard/u_id > pc / id_ex.rs2_val. That is the EX-stage redirect (fwd
compare -> fwd mux -> 32-bit branch compare -> misalign -> redirect) feeding
if_stage's "(flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data" mux. That one mux puts
`redirect` in front of EVERYTHING that reads the fetched instruction: the
regfile read address (the report even starts at cpu/u_rf/regs_*), the
decoder, imm_gen, the load-use comparators in hazard_unit (-> stall_if ->
pc mux / ID/EX CE) and the ID/EX data flops. So the loop is
EX-resolve + regfile-read + bypass + hazard + reset-mux chained in a single
cycle (46 LUT levels), even though none of it is functionally needed:
load-use needs a LOAD in EX while redirect needs a branch/JAL/JALR in EX,
so they are mutually exclusive, and flush_id already zeroes ID/EX on
every redirect that is not under a dmem stall (where ID/EX is held anyway).
Mispredict penalty is only 1 cycle (IF/ID is combinational), so we do not
want to add redirect latency; we want the same 1-cycle penalty with the
redirect fan-out cut down to the pc mux and a narrow flush.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Structural re-timing of the redirect loop, same architectural behaviour and
same cycle count (CPI unchanged, retirement order and RVFI unchanged):

1. Take `redirect` off the instruction path. if_stage drives
   out.instr = imem_stall ? NOP : imem_data and out.valid = !imem_stall;
   hazard_unit.flush_if becomes just `!imem_ready` (no redirect term).
   The wrong-path instruction that sits in IF/ID in the redirect cycle is
   killed by the existing flush_id at the ID/EX register (redirect implies
   the EX op is a branch/jump, so md_stall is 0 and load_use is 0; the only
   other case is dmem_stall where ID/EX is held and the identical redirect
   re-fires until the stall clears, exactly as today). The regfile address,
   decoder, imm_gen and load-use comparators now hang off the imem_data
   flop/bus only, and `redirect` fans out to just pc-mux, flush_id (ID/EX
   control reset) and nothing deeper.
2. Narrow the flush/bubble resets. ID/EX on flush and EX/MEM on md_stall
   bubble clear only `valid` and the ctrl_t bundle (reg_write, mem_read,
   mem_write, is_branch, is_jump, alu_op->0, is_illegal ...) instead of
   zeroing all ~230 data flops. Data fields become plain CE flops (no sync
   reset mux in the D path) and flush_id fan-out drops from ~230 to ~25.
   Reset-time zeroing of the full struct is kept (reset still clears all) so
   RVFI/X behaviour on invalid slots is unchanged; invalid slots never
   retire.
3. Precompute the PC-relative target in ID. id_stage adds pc + imm once
   (imm_gen -> 32-bit adder -> ID/EX) and registers `tgt` and `tgt_misal`
   (= tgt[1:0] != 0) plus `pc_plus4` (if_stage already forms pc+4). EX no
   longer contains the pc+imm adder: branch/JAL redirect_target =
   is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],0} : in.tgt, link value = in.pc_plus4,
   fall-through pc_next = in.pc_plus4, and misalign_fault collapses to
   (branch_taken & tgt_misal) | (is_jump & (is_jalr ? jalr_sum[1] :
   tgt_misal)), which is 2-3 LUT levels instead of waiting on the adder.
   JALR keeps its own rs1+imm adder in EX (only jalr_sum[1:0] is needed for
   the misalign check). Cost ~66 extra flops + one 32-bit adder moved
   from EX to ID; the design is at 2446 / 10000 LUT4 so area is a non-issue.
4. Link/alu_result mux: the EX/MEM alu_result D input today is
   is_jump ? pc+4 : md_op ? md_result : alu_result, i.e. two mux levels
   after the ALU op mux. Merge the is_jump and md_op legs into one
   registered-select 3:1 (sel from ID/EX flops, available at cycle start),
   using in.pc_plus4 for the link value, so only a single LUT level follows
   the ALU result.

Expected effect: the longest chain becomes ID/EX flop -> fwd select ->
fwd mux -> compare -> redirect -> pc mux (~10-12 LUT levels) rather than
that chain + regfile RAM read + bypass + hazard + reset mux (46 levels), so
Fmax moves from ~52 MHz towards 60-70 MHz with iter/cycle unchanged.
If a different path (dmem read -> load align -> MEM/WB, or the 33x33
multiplier) becomes the next limiter the gain saturates there, which is why
the confidence is only medium.

title: Zero-bubble fetch predecode predictor (JAL + BTFN + EX-trained RAS) with 1-bit mispredict check and redirect-decoupled IF
motivation:
The muldiv core (110.5 iter/s, 51.7 MHz, ~468k cycles/iter) still pays a one-slot
fetch bubble on EVERY taken branch / JAL / JALR: redirect is resolved in EX and
flushes the slot being fetched. CoreMark has ~14 such redirects per 100 instructions
(loop back-edges, calls, returns, forward-taken ifs) and the only previous predictor
attempt (hyp-20261001-003-r1s2, stateless JAL+BTFN+RAS predecode) measured +5.6%
iterations/cycle on the old 5.4 MHz core. It lost the round only because the muldiv
Fmax fix landed in the same tournament. LESSONS.md says to re-test fetch-side
predictors on the 51.7 MHz core because their extra paths (imem_data -> predecode ->
adder -> pc mux, and fwd -> JALR add -> 32-bit compare -> redirect) can become
critical. The r1s2 design compared a 32-bit predicted next-pc against the actual
next-pc in EX (adder + 32-bit compare behind the forwarding mux), which is exactly
the kind of path that would cost Fmax here. This hypothesis keeps the IPC win but
designs the verification so that it adds ~0 logic depth to the existing EX redirect
cone and removes redirect from the IF->hazard->ID/EX control chain (which is the
current Gowin worst path. Re-measured with `make timing` on this checkout: Fmax
49.7 MHz at place option 0, worst path 25.4 ns / 46 cells, ID/EX rs value ->
EX forward mux + branch compare -> redirect -> IF NOP gating of the fetched
instruction -> rs1/rs2 load-use compare in hazard_unit -> stall_id/flush_id ->
ID/EX capture (hierarchy trace: u_id > u_ex > u_if > u_id > u_if > u_hazard > u_id,
with pc_* flops as co-critical endpoints). All top-5 paths are this same
redirect-to-control chain, so cutting the cells between `redirect` and the ID/EX
enable is a direct Fmax lever, while the predictor makes `redirect` rarer.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1. IF-stage predecode (rtl/if_stage.sv). On the fetched word imem_data (already
   combinational from the pc register):
     * JAL (opcode 1101111): predict taken, target = pc + J-imm, only if
       instr[21]==0 (target 4-byte aligned, so EX never raises a misalign trap on a
       predicted-taken JAL).
     * BRANCH (opcode 1100011): predict taken iff instr[31]==1 (backward, BTFN) and
       instr[8]==0 (aligned). Forward branches stay predicted not-taken.
     * 'ret' = JALR with rd==x0, rs1 in {x1,x5}, instr[31:20]==0 and RAS non-empty:
       predict taken, target = RAS top (RAS entries are pc+4 of calls, so aligned).
     next_pc priority: redirect (EX) > predicted target > pc+4. imem_addr stays a plain
     register output of pc. The predicted-taken decision is qualified by the
     (imem_stall-NOPed) instruction, so bubbles never carry pred_taken=1. Branch/JAL
     predicted target = pc + imm uses the same formula as EX's branch_target, so
     pred_target need NOT be carried for them: the pc advance and the ID/EX capture
     happen on exactly the same edges (a valid instruction is only captured when
     !stall_id, which implies !stall_if), so the only fact EX needs is the 1-bit
     pred_taken (added to if_id_t / id_ex_t in rtl/core_pkg.sv and captured in
     rtl/id_stage.sv). For predicted rets also carry pred_target[31:2] (30 flops) in
     id_ex_t.
2. EX-stage verification (rtl/ex_stage.sv), 1-bit based instead of a 32-bit next-pc
   compare:
       act_redirect = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault   // as today
       ret_bad      = pred_taken && is_jalr &&
                      !(rs1[31:2] == pred_target[31:2] && !rs1[1])  // BEQ-depth eq on
                                                                    // the forwarded rs1
       mispredict   = in.valid && ((act_redirect != pred_taken) || ret_bad)
       redirect         = mispredict
       redirect_target  = act_redirect ? (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
                                       : in.pc + 4   // predicted-taken but not taken
     Every case is covered: correct taken prediction (no redirect, zero bubble),
     correct not-taken, taken-but-predicted-not (1 bubble, same as today),
     predicted-taken-but-fell-through / non-branch alias under symbolic formal
     instruction streams (redirect to pc+4), JALR target mismatch (redirect to
     jump_target), misaligned trap (act_redirect=0, so redirect iff predicted taken,
     to pc+4, matching reg_q.pc_next which already reverts to pc+4). RVFI pc_next /
     pc_wdata logic is untouched (actual next pc), so riscv-formal pc_fwd / unique /
     liveness / ill see unchanged architectural behaviour.
3. RAS trained at EX, never at IF (rtl/if_stage.sv + rtl/ex_stage.sv or a small new
   rtl/ras.sv): 4 x 30-bit shift-register stack + 3-bit saturating depth. EX pushes
   pc+4 when a valid, non-stalled (!stall_ex_mem && !md_stall) JAL/JALR with rd in
   {x1,x5} commits, and pops when a valid non-stalled ret-pattern JALR commits.
   Updating from resolved correct-path instructions means NO wrong-path pollution
   and no dependency of RAS enables on the redirect signal. Stale reads in tight
   call/ret sequences only cost a mispredict, never correctness, because every
   prediction is verified in EX.
4. Redirect-decoupled IF (rtl/if_stage.sv, rtl/hazard_unit.sv): today
   out.instr/out.valid are forced to NOP on `redirect`, which puts the late EX
   redirect signal in front of the rs1/rs2 load-use compare in hazard_unit and then
   in front of stall_id/flush_id and the ~190-flop ID/EX enable. That NOP-ing is
   redundant: whenever redirect=1, ID/EX either flushes to zero (flush_id wins over
   stall in id_stage) or holds (dmem/md stall) and PC takes redirect_target with
   priority, so the IF payload is ignored. Gate the IF payload only on imem_stall
   (flush_if = imem_stall) and let load_use be computed from the raw instruction;
   flush_id = (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall && !md_stall is unchanged and a
   spurious load-use during redirect is masked by flush priority. This removes ~3-4
   LUT levels (instr mux -> 2x 5-bit compare -> or/and) after `redirect` on the
   worst path.
Predictor state is deliberately tiny: 120 + 30 + a few flops, ~100-150 LUTs; no
tables, no BTB tags, no BHT aliasing. Non-ret JALR and forward-taken branches still
cost the existing 1-slot bubble.
Expected: ~65% of redirects removed. With ~22% imem stalls absorbing some bubbles,
r1s2 measured +5.6% iter/cycle for the same predictor coverage; the 1-bit verify
and the decoupled IF should keep Fmax at >= 51.7 MHz (possibly higher because the
redirect->flush->hazard chain shortens). Fallback ordering if the implementation
agent sees timing trouble: drop the RAS first (keep JAL + BTFN), keep items 2 and 4.

changes.description: Add pred_taken to if_id_t and id_ex_t, and pred_target[31:2] to id_ex_t (used only for predicted rets).

Predecode imem_data (JAL, backward branch BTFN, ret via RAS top); next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4; export pred_taken/pred_target; gate the NOP payload on imem_stall only (not on redirect).
Capture pred_taken and pred_target into the ID/EX register alongside the existing payload.

title: Dedicated rs1+imm address register for dmem: take ALU op mux and result select off the BSRAM address path
motivation:
Re-ran `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (60.8-63.2 MHz). The top-5 worst paths all end at
a dmem BSRAM address pin (dmem_N_dmem_N_0_0_s/ADB[10]) and start at the regfile BSRAM output
(cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s/DO, tC2Q 2.26 ns; Gowin absorbed the ID/EX rs?_val register into the
regfile BSRAM's synchronous read port) or at the forward-unit compare. The 14-cell path is:
BSRAM DO -> x0/write-bypass LUT -> 3 forward-mux LUTs -> alu_a auipc mux -> 2 ALU LUTs ->
FIVE result_sel LUT levels (19-way ALU op case mux + jump/muldiv select) -> stall-hold mux LUT ->
1.2 ns net -> dmem BSRAM ADB. dmem_addr is just the EX/MEM.alu_result flop; the wrapper's dmem is
an async-read array on that registered address, so the flop is absorbed into the BSRAM address
register and the whole EX cone (including the ALU op mux) ends at the BSRAM address setup.
For LOAD/STORE the address is simply rs1_fwd + imm, and alu_result of a load/store is never used
for anything else (loads write read_data via the mem_to_reg mux, stores write nothing, a load is
never forwarded from EX/MEM because of the load-use bubble). The alu_a/alu_b operand muxes, the
ALU op mux and result_sel are pure overhead on the address path (about 7 of the 14 cells).

title: Split dmem address generation (AGU) out of the ALU result mux and pre-decode ALU result select
motivation:
After the redirect-off-IF/ID cut the champion's worst path (21.7 ns arrival,
14 logic cells, 63 MHz; log.jsonl hyp-001-r2s0 and hyp-002-r2s1, all 25
reported worst paths) is regfile RAM output -> EX forward mux -> alu_a/alu_b
mux -> 32-bit ALU adder -> 11-arm ALU result case mux -> jump/muldiv
result_sel -> EX/MEM.alu_result, and that register IS the dmem BSRAM address
(io_dmemAddr = ex_mem.alu_result), so the endpoint is the dmem BSRAM address
pin (cpu/u_rf/regs_* -> dmem_N_dmem_N_0_0_s). The dmem address only needs
base+imm, yet it currently waits behind everything the ALU result path does:
the alu_a (AUIPC) mux, the ALU op case mux (SUB, SLT, SLTU, shifts, logic,
LUI all in one case) and the jump/MUL link mux. ex_stage already contains
exactly the adder an address generator needs (`jalr_sum = rs1 + in.imm`, fed
directly by the forwarded rs1, no alu_a/alu_b/result muxes), and it is used
only for the JALR target. This is a structural separation of the
address-generation unit from the ALU result datapath, not a retiming of
existing logic, and is orthogonal to the already-banked redirect cut.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1. Dedicated AGU = the existing JALR adder. Add `agu_addr [31:0]` to
   ex_mem_t (core_pkg.sv) and register `agu_addr <= jalr_sum` (= forwarded
   rs1 + in.imm) in ex_stage.sv. For every LOAD/STORE alu_src=1 so this equals
   the ALU's ADD result exactly; for other instructions it is a don't-care
   (dmem_ren/dmem_wen are already gated by ctrl, and dmem_addr was already
   arbitrary ALU output on non-memory instructions). Keep ex_mem.alu_result
   as is (forwarding / writeback / RVFI), so no behaviour change.
2. mem_stage.sv: drive io_dmemAddr from `in.agu_addr` and take every
   address-derived quantity (byte_mask, misalign check, aligned RVFI
   mem_addr, load shift amount `addr[1:0]*8`) from `in.agu_addr` instead of
   `in.alu_result`. The dmem BSRAM address register then hangs off
   BSRAM -> fwd mux -> one carry chain only (about 4 LUT levels shorter than
   today: no alu_a mux, no ALU case mux, no result_sel mux), and
   ex_mem.alu_result becomes an ordinary fabric flop (smaller setup than the
   BSRAM address pin) used only for forwarding and writeback.
3. Cut the depth that is left on the alu_result path so the AGU split is not
   just moving the critical path 1 ns sideways: (a) decode the ALU result
   select into registered one-hot controls in id_stage (sel_add, sel_logic,
   sel_shift, sel_slt, sel_lui, plus sub / logic-op bits) carried in ctrl_t
   (alu_op stays for muldiv and the ALTOPS branch), so the final ALU mux is
   an AND-OR from flop selects instead of a 5-bit op decode; (b) share one
   adder for ADD/SUB/SLT/SLTU in alu.sv: sum = a + (b ^ {32{sub}}) + sub with
   a 33-bit extension, SLTU = ~carry_out, SLT = overflow-corrected sign, so
   the case mux has one add arm instead of three separate carry chains
   (a+b, a-b, two comparators); (c) fold the AUIPC pc and imm operand
   selection into one 2-level AND-OR with the forward mux where the
   selects (is_auipc, alu_src, fwd_sel) are all flop/early signals. ALTOPS
   stand-in arms and the muldiv interface in alu.sv stay untouched.
Cycle counts are identical (no pipeline-depth change, same stalls), so the
fitness delta is pure Fmax. The AGU split alone is expected to move the
dmem-address endpoint off the critical list; item 3 trims the next-worst
alu_result path (shifter / SLT / adder arms) so the net Fmax gain clears the
~6% place-and-route seed spread. Cost: +32 flops and a few dozen LUTs
(design is 2409 / 10000 LUT4), no new DSP/BSRAM. Correctness: formal and
cosim must stay identical because agu_addr == alu_result on every
load/store and RVFI mem_addr is derived from the same value; misaligned
access trap logic only changes its source net.

title: PC-indexed 16-entry taken-only BTB with next-PC-compare verify (no imem_data predecode in fetch)
motivation:
Every taken branch/JAL/JALR still costs one bubble: the redirect is resolved in EX and
flushes the instruction being fetched/decoded (IF+ID is a single combinational cycle here,
so the penalty is exactly 1 slot). CoreMark has ~14 such redirects per 100 instructions.
The only predictor measured on the current core (r2s2: JAL + BTFN + EX-trained RAS predecode)
removed 5.3% of the cycles (4.68M -> 4.43M) but lost 12% Fmax (63.2 -> 55.8 MHz), because it
put imem_data -> predecode -> target adder/RAS -> pc mux in the fetch cone and a pred_target /
RAS flop bank next to it. LESSONS.md concludes "drop fetch-side prediction" -- but that
conclusion is about *instruction-bits-driven* predecode. A PC-indexed BTB is a different
circuit: the lookup depends only on the pc flops (pc -> small tag compare -> pc mux), so the
imem_data -> decode -> pc path of the champion is untouched, it learns forward-taken branches
and call/jump targets that a static BTFN/JAL rule cannot, and the verification can be done
entirely from flops that are already in ID/EX (no pred_taken/pred_target bundle fields).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a tiny taken-only BTB inside if_stage and verify every prediction in EX by comparing the
*fetch PC register* with the architecturally correct next PC. The champion's critical path is
regfile -> forward mux -> ALU -> dmem address (~21.7 ns, 14 cells); none of the new logic sits
on it, and the EX redirect cone stays at ~the same depth.

1. BTB (if_stage.sv): 16 entries, direct-mapped on pc[5:2]; per entry valid(1) +
   partial tag pc[13:6] (8) + partial target [19:2] (18), plain flops (~430 FF, no RAM
   inference). hit = valid[idx] && tag[idx] == pc[13:6]; pred_pc = {pc[31:20], tgt[idx], 2'b00}.
   next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : (hit ? pred_pc : pc_plus4). Because *every* prediction
   is checked against the real next PC in EX, partial tags / partial targets / aliasing /
   false hits on non-control instructions only cost performance, never correctness, and the
   BTB needs no bits carried down the pipeline. The ID/EX struct gets no new fields.
2. Verify in EX (ex_stage.sv): new input fetch_pc (= if_id_w.pc, a flop). Invariant: while a
   valid instruction I sits in EX, the pc register holds the address that was fetched after I
   (pc only advances on the cycle I is captured; a stall holds both; a redirect rewrites it).
   eq_tgt = (fetch_pc[31:2] == in.tgt[31:2]); eq_ft = (fetch_pc[31:2] == in.pc_plus4[31:2]) --
   both from flops, so a 3-level compare running in parallel with the late forward->branch-cond
   chain. Define actual_taken = (is_branch && branch_cond) || is_jump; exp_ft = !actual_taken ||
   misalign_fault (trap keeps the linear PC, as today). actual_next = (is_jalr && !misalign) ?
   jalr_target : exp_ft ? pc_plus4 : in.tgt. redirect = in.valid && ((is_jalr && !misalign) ||
   (exp_ft ? !eq_ft : !eq_tgt)); redirect_target = actual_next. JALR is never predicted (always
   redirects, exactly as today) so no 32-bit compare ever sits behind the forward mux + JALR adder.
   A predicted-taken branch that resolves not-taken redirects to pc+4 (1 bubble = today's cost
   of a taken branch); a BTB false hit on a non-control instruction does the same.
   reg_q.pc_next <= actual_next (NOT redirect ? target : pc+4, since a correct prediction no
   longer redirects) so rvfi_pc_wdata stays architectural.
3. Training (registered, off the critical cone): from the EX/MEM register (ex_mem_w), when
   valid && !ctrl.is_illegal: a taken branch (is_branch && branch_taken) or JAL
   (is_jump && !is_jalr) writes entry pc[5:2] with {1, pc[13:6], branch_target[19:2]}; a
   not-taken branch (is_branch && !branch_taken) clears valid[pc[5:2]] if the stored tag
   matches. Using EX/MEM keeps the late branch condition out of the BTB write-enable fan-out
   (~430 flops); the one-cycle training delay is irrelevant. Writes are idempotent so a
   dmem-stall hold of EX/MEM is harmless.
4. Hazard (hazard_unit.sv): flush_id = (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall && !md_stall.
   The old "redirect implies no md_stall" argument no longer holds because a false BTB hit on
   a MUL/DIV in EX redirects; without the extra term the flush would kill the held MUL/DIV.
   A load in EX with a false-hit successor is fine (both load-use and redirect bubble ID/EX,
   redirect has priority on the pc). Under dmem/md stall the redirect fires once, rewrites
   pc, and the next cycle's compare matches, so there is no repeated redirect.

Expected effect: CoreMark's hot taken branches are tight loop back-edges (crc, matrix, list
walk), JALs and a few forward-taken ifs; a 16-entry taken-only BTB should remove ~40-55% of the
taken-redirect bubbles (~14/100 instr, partly hidden under the 22% imem stalls) -> ~4-6% fewer
cycles (r2s2's static scheme got 5.3%), at roughly flat Fmax because the added cones are
flop-to-flop and shorter than the ALU/dmem path. Net expectation is modest (the P&R seed
spread is ~6%), which is why confidence is low; the downside risk is bounded since cycles can
only go down vs. the champion unless the BTB thrashes, and mispredicts cost the same 1 slot
as today's taken branches.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r3s2 (improvement, +6.77%): A 16-entry PC-indexed taken-only BTB (lookup from pc flops only, partial tag/target, trained from EX/MEM) verified in EX by comparing the pc register against the architectural next PC (`eq_tgt`/`eq_ft`, JALR always redirects) reached 144.10 (+6.77%, barely above the ~6% P&R seed spread) where the imem_data-driven JAL/BTFN/RAS predecode of r2s2 netted zero-to-negative, so fetch-side prediction is only worth its Fmax cost when it stays off the imem_data->decode->pc path and adds no pred_taken/pred_target bits to ID/EX (no cycles/Fmax split was recorded, so attribution is inferred); because a false BTB hit now makes a MUL/DIV or non-control instruction redirect, `flush_id` must also be gated by `!md_stall` and `reg_q.pc_next` must be the architectural `actual_next` rather than `redirect ? target : pc+4`, and larger/associative BTBs should be judged against the ~430-flop cost already paid.

title: ID-precomputed one-hot forward/operand selects: remove fwd compare and alu_src/auipc mux level from the EX front
motivation:
The champion's worst path (log.jsonl hyp-20261001-003-r3s2: 21.499 ns,
26 cells / 17 logic levels, 63.7 MHz) is
cpu/u_id/reg_q.rs2_addr -> cpu/u_fwd -> cpu/u_ex -> u_alu -> u_ex -> dmem BSRAM
address pin. It starts at the ID/EX rs?_addr flops and runs through the
forward_unit comparators (id_ex.rs? vs ex_mem.rd / mem_wb.rd, reg_write and
x0 qualification, EX/MEM-over-MEM/WB priority: about 2-3 LUT levels), then
the 3:1 forward data mux, then the separate alu_a (auipc ? pc : rs1) /
alu_b (alu_src ? imm : rs2) 2:1 level, then the adder, the ALU op mux and
result_sel. The comparison result depends only on instruction fields that
are already known one cycle earlier, in ID, so it is pure redundant depth on
the shared front of every EX cone (ALU result, branch compare -> redirect,
jalr_sum, dmem address). r3s0 showed that shortening a single endpoint
(dmem address) is capped by sibling endpoints; this change cuts the shared
head instead, which helps all of them.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decide the forwarding source and the ALU operand source in ID, one cycle
early, and register them as one-hot select flops in ID/EX, so the EX
operand muxes are driven straight from flops: no id_ex.rs?_addr compares,
no priority logic, and no extra alu_src/auipc mux level in front of the adder.

ID side (id_stage.sv, with a few extra inputs from core.sv). For the
instruction I in ID (rs1 = instr[19:15], rs2 = instr[24:20]), the pipeline
one cycle later has I-1 in EX/MEM and I-2 in MEM/WB, so per source operand:
  m1 = id_ex.ctrl.reg_write && id_ex.rd != 0 && id_ex.rd == rs   // I-1 -> forward EX/MEM.alu_result
  m2 = ex_mem_rw_post_mem_trap && ex_mem.rd != 0 && ex_mem.rd == rs   // I-2 -> forward wb_w_data
and register (under exactly the ID/EX data-field enable, !stall_id):
  fwd_ex_q = m1 && !misalign_fault_ex     (I-1 trapping in EX gets reg_write cleared in EX/MEM, so it must not forward)
  fwd_wb_q = m2 && !fwd_ex_d               (exclusive one-hot; EX/MEM priority preserved, and a trapped I-1 falls through to I-2 exactly like the old live logic)
where ex_mem_rw_post_mem_trap is mem_stage's ctrl_with_trap.reg_write (a
MEM-stage misaligned load/store clears reg_write in MEM/WB, which the old
live forward_unit saw) and misalign_fault_ex is exported by ex_stage.
The shift argument: ID/EX captures only on cycles where EX/MEM and MEM/WB
also advance. dmem_stall and md_stall block the capture (stall_id) and freeze
the whole pipe, so the held selects stay valid; a load-use bubble makes I-1
a ctrl=0 bubble so the load matches as I-2 and forwards from wb_w_data in the
next cycle; redirect only kills wrong-path ID/EX contents. MUL/DIV operands
are latched by muldiv on the first EX cycle, which is the only cycle the
selects are guaranteed fresh for, exactly as today.

Operand-source selects for the ALU (separate from the rs1/rs2 forward
muxes, which are still needed for branch compare, jalr_sum, store data,
muldiv and RVFI): register a_sel_pc = is_auipc, b_sel_imm = alu_src, and the
gated forwards a_ex = fwd_ex_q && !auipc, a_wb = fwd_wb_q && !auipc,
b_ex = fwd_ex_q && !alu_src, b_wb = fwd_wb_q && !alu_src (computed in ID from
the decoder outputs, which are already available there). EX then forms
alu_a = one-hot{pc, ex_mem.alu_result, wb_w_data, in.rs1_val} and
alu_b = one-hot{imm, ex_mem.alu_result, wb_w_data, in.rs2_val} in a single
4:1 AND-OR level (Gowin MUX2_LUT5/LUT4), replacing forward-mux -> 2:1 mux.
rs1 = fwd_ex_q ? ex_mem.alu_result : fwd_wb_q ? fwd_mem_wb : in.rs1_val
(selects are raw flops). forward_unit.sv is removed (core.sv wires the new
signals); ~10 new ID/EX flops and ~64 duplicated mux LUTs (LUT4 count is not
scored; no net cycle change).

Expected effect: 3 fewer logic levels at the head of the dmem-address /
ALU-result / redirect cones (~2-3 ns of the 21.5 ns path), identical cycle
count (same stall/bubble schedule, no architectural change). Risks: (1) the
new ID-side compares hang off imem_data, but at the same depth as the
existing load-use comparators that already sit on that input in hazard_unit;
(2) the misalign_fault -> select-flop D kill has the same depth as the
existing misalign_fault -> EX/MEM ctrl.reg_write flop, but if it ends up on
the worst path, fall back to qualifying with the registered
ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write in EX (one LUT on the select path only; data paths
unchanged); (3) other near-critical cones (regfile BSRAM DO -> bypass ->
mux -> pc redirect) also lose the alu_src/auipc level but not the data-side
mux, so the realised gain may be capped below the ideal. Verification:
existing riscv-formal (reg / pc_fwd / ill / unique / liveness), cosim and
test_alu cocotb should pass unchanged because RVFI-visible behaviour
is identical.

title: Resolve forwarding in ID: register per-operand EX/MEM and MEM/WB match flags so EX has no register-address compare
motivation:
The champion's reported worst path (hyp-20261001-003-r3s2: 21.499 ns arrival, 26 cells / 17
logic levels, 63.7 MHz) starts at cpu/u_id/reg_q.rs2_addr_2 (an ID/EX *address* flop), runs
through cpu/u_fwd -> cpu/u_ex -> cpu/u_ex/u_alu -> cpu/u_ex and ends at the dmem BSRAM
address pin. In other words the cone begins with forward_unit's combinational 5-bit
register-address compares (id_ex_rs? vs ex_mem_rd / mem_wb_rd, gated by reg_write and
rd != 0, then an EX/MEM-over-MEM/WB priority), costing ~3 LUT levels plus the high-fanout
select nets (each select drives 32 mux bits plus the branch comparator, JALR adder and
store-data path) BEFORE the 3:1 operand mux, the AUIPC/imm operand mux, the ALU and the
result select. r3s0's analysis shows the other start point (regfile BSRAM DO -> bypass ->
forward mux) is only ~1.5-2 ns behind, so the compare front is the one removable piece of
the *shared* front end (r3s0/r3s1 attacked only the unshared tail and got +4.28% / -3.22%).
The compares depend only on register numbers that are already known one cycle earlier,
while the instruction sits in ID, so they can be done there at no cost to the EX cone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move the forwarding *address* compares from EX into ID and register their results in the
ID/EX register, leaving EX with a flop-driven, pre-decoded 2-level operand mux. Behaviour
is cycle-for-cycle identical to the current forward_unit (same priority, same x0 handling,
same fault/trap gating), so cycles/iteration are unchanged (4.42M) and only Fmax moves.

Timing of the compares. When instruction X is in ID (cycle c), the instruction E that is in
ID/EX will be in EX/MEM when X is in EX, and the instruction M that is in EX/MEM will be in
MEM/WB. X is captured into ID/EX only when stall_id=0, and in exactly that case EX/MEM
captures E and MEM/WB captures M (every stall source - dmem_stall, md_stall - also asserts
stall_id, and load-use turns E into a bubble in ID/EX with X re-decoded next cycle), so the
compare against (ID/EX.rd, EX/MEM.rd) at ID time equals the compare the old forward_unit made
against (EX/MEM.rd, MEM/WB.rd) at EX time. Hold cycles (dmem_stall freezes ID/EX, EX/MEM and
the MEM/WB data fields) keep the flags consistent; md_stall only matters on the first EX
cycle because muldiv latches its operands on `start`.

Changes:
1. core_pkg.sv: add four flags to id_ex_t: m1_rs1, m2_rs1, m1_rs2, m2_rs2 (4 flops).
2. forward_unit.sv (file kept, interface changed): purely ID-side. Inputs if_id_rs1/rs2
   (instr[19:15]/[24:20]), id_ex_rd, ex_mem_rd. Outputs m1_rs1 = (id_ex_rd == rs1 && rd != 0),
   m2_rs1 = (ex_mem_rd == rs1 && rd != 0) and the same for rs2. The id_ex_rd == rs? terms are
   the same comparators hazard_unit already builds for load-use, so synthesis shares them.
   NO reg_write / valid gating here.
3. id_stage.sv: new inputs ex_mem_rd; instantiate forward_unit on in.instr and reg_q.rd;
   capture the four flags in the ID/EX register with the same `!stall` enable as the data
   fields (reset to 0 with the rest of the struct; a flush bubble need not clear them because
   ctrl.reg_write=0 / valid=0 make the instruction inert).
4. ex_stage.sv: replace fwd_rs1_sel/fwd_rs2_sel with ex_mem_we / mem_wb_we inputs
   (ex_mem_w.ctrl.reg_write, mem_wb_w.ctrl.reg_write - the already-trap-gated flops). The
   operand muxes become
      use1 = in.m1_rsX & ex_mem_we;  use2 = in.m2_rsX & mem_wb_we;
      rsX  = use1 ? fwd_ex_mem : use2 ? fwd_mem_wb : in.rsX_val;
   i.e. two LUT4 levels whose select inputs come straight from flops (no compare, no priority
   encoder, no 2-bit select decode). The live reg_write gating is kept in EX on purpose so a
   misaligned JAL/JALR/branch (EX fault clears EX/MEM reg_write) or misaligned load (MEM fault
   clears MEM/WB reg_write) still falls through to the next-older source / regfile value
   exactly as today, which the riscv-formal reg/pc checks require.
5. core.sv: wire ex_mem_w.rd into id_stage, ex_mem_w.ctrl.reg_write / mem_wb_w.ctrl.reg_write
   into ex_stage, drop fwd_rs?_sel wires.

Expected effect: removes ~3 LUT levels and the select-decode fanout from the head of the
worst cone (~2.5-3.5 ns of the 21.5 ns arrival); the BSRAM-DO start point caps the gain at the
~1.5-2 ns gap, i.e. roughly 63.7 -> 69-71 MHz (+8-11%) at unchanged IPC. Cost: 4 ID/EX flops,
two extra 5-bit compare pairs on the imem_data -> flop-D path (flop endpoints, not BSRAM
setup, so well inside the period) and about the same LUT count as today. Risks: P&R seed
spread (~6%) and the new flag flops' fanout; each flag drives 32 operand-mux bits + the
branch comparator, but unlike the old selects they are flop outputs that placement can sit
next to the muxes (and the flags can be duplicated per consumer if needed).

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r4s1 (regression, -4.13%): Moving the forward address compares into ID but registering only raw match flags (`m1_rs?`/`m2_rs?`) and leaving the live `& ex_mem_we` / `& mem_wb_we` gating plus the EX/MEM-over-MEM/WB priority chain in ex_stage scored 138.15, below the 144.10 champion, while same-round r4s0 registered fully pre-decoded one-hot selects (gating, priority and a_sel/b_sel folded in ID) for 150.95 (+4.75%) with identical cycles; since both variants have the same ID-side compare cost, the ~9% gap (above the ~6% P&R seed spread, no post-change worst-path report to confirm) points to the residual EX-side AND + priority decode (still two LUT4 levels, with ex_mem_we/mem_wb_we each fanning out to four gates) cancelling the saved compare, so if the forwarding front is revisited, register final one-hot selects and keep nothing but a flat AND-OR in EX, and expect at most ~+5% since the compare front is not the 2.5-3.5 ns the estimate assumed.

title: BTB-directed run-ahead fetch: 4-entry fetch queue lets the predicted PC stream keep fetching through backend stalls
motivation:
I replayed the CoreMark retirement trace (2.92M instrs, 4.42M cycles in the timed window) against
the champion's 16-entry BTB. The model reproduces the redirect penalty exactly (1 cycle per
redirect; 357K redirects without BTB -> 100K with it = the 259K cycles the BTB saved) and
calibrates the whole pipeline to 4.43M cycles (actual 4.42M) from just: 22% imem stall with pc
held, 22% dmem stall on loads/stores, 2 stall cycles per MUL (94K), 1 per load-use (204K), 1 per
redirect. Consequence for the predictor category: a PERFECT branch/return predictor can remove
at most the remaining 100K redirect cycles (2.3% of cycles); a 64-entry 2-bit BTB + RAS only
gets to ~58K redirects (~0.95%). Direction/target prediction is therefore exhausted below the 4.6%
acceptance bar. The dominant remaining loss is different: ~0.22 of every cycle is an imem stall
and the pc is HELD whenever the backend stalls (dmem stall, load-use, MUL), so the fetch slots
during ~0.6M backend-stall cycles are thrown away. The predicted-PC stream (BTB + pc+4) can
run ahead of the backend if fetched instructions are parked in a small queue.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decouple fetch from decode with a 4-entry fetch queue whose entries are {pc, instr, pred_next},
where pred_next is the next-PC the BTB/pc+4 mux chose when that entry was fetched. Fetch (pc
register, imem_addr = pc unchanged) advances whenever imem_ready and the queue has room or the
ID stage consumes this cycle, regardless of stall_id. ID takes the queue head, or the
imem_data BYPASS when the queue is empty (so the no-stall path and the 1-cycle redirect
penalty are unchanged; the only added logic on the imem_data->decode path is one 2:1 mux
selected by a flop, q_empty). When ID cannot consume (stall_id from dmem stall / load-use /
md_stall) a successfully fetched instruction is pushed to the queue instead of being dropped
and re-fetched. Offline replay of the exact trace + 22% stall model: depth 0 = 4.43M cycles
(matches silicon-sim 4.42M), depth 2 = 4.15M (-6.2%), depth 3 = 4.106M (-7.3%), depth 4 =
4.093M (-7.6%) => +6.5..8% iterations/cycle, with the BTB/redirect behavior unchanged. This
is a predictor-category change because the BTB-predicted PC stream is what runs ahead; the queue
is the structure that lets the prediction hide stall latency (fetch-directed prefetch).

Required changes for correctness:
1. Next-PC verify must move off the live pc register (which now runs ahead of the instruction in
   EX). Carry 30-bit pred_next (the next_pc fetch used right after this instruction) through
   the queue into ID/EX (add to if_id_t and id_ex_t, ~30 flops) and in ex_stage compute
   eq_tgt = (in.pred_next == in.tgt[31:2]) and eq_ft = (in.pred_next == in.pc_plus4[31:2])
   instead of fetch_pc. Same compare structure/depth as today (flop-to-flop in parallel with
   the branch-condition chain); JALR still always redirects.
2. A redirect flushes the queue (count <= 0, pc <= redirect_target) and flush_id kills the
   wrong-path instruction in IF/ID as today. Because the verify now compares a registered
   per-instruction pred_next, a mispredicted instruction HELD in EX under dmem/md stall would
   re-fire redirect every stall cycle (it used to fire once because pc was rewritten). Add a
   1-bit redir_done flop (set when redirect fires while stall_id/md_stall holds ID/EX,
   cleared when ID/EX advances) and fold !redir_done into the early redir_c0/redir_c1 terms
   so the late branch_cond select is untouched. JALR in a held EX likewise redirects once.
3. Queue is flushed by redirect (higher priority than push/pop, as pc already is). Keep the
   existing pc priority: redirect > fetch-advance. Fetch-advance condition replaces `!stall`
   with `imem_ready && (q_count < 4 || id_consume)`, where id_consume = !stall_id (known from
   the same early signals as today's stall).
4. RVFI: pc_rdata/insn are captured per entry, so retirement order and pc_wdata (= resolved
   architectural next PC, already actual_next in EX) stay exactly as now; rvfi_order is untouched.

title: Take the regfile BSRAM read and the WB result mux off the EX front: fabric-flop regfile + pre-muxed MEM/WB write-back data
motivation:
Fresh `make timing` on the champion (63.45 MHz this placement, 15.76 ns period) shows the top-25
setup paths are two tied families, both within 0.2 ns of each other:
  (1) cpu/u_rf/regs BSRAM DO -> id_ex.rs1_val bypass LUT x2 -> ex rs1 fwd mux -> alu_a -> adder ->
      result_sel -> dmem BSRAM address (21.055 ns arrival, 14 cells). Gowin inferred the
      32x32 regfile as BSRAM and absorbed the ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val flops into it, so in EX the
      operand starts at a BSRAM clk->DO of 2.26 ns (a fabric flop is 0.23 ns) and then pays two
      extra LUT levels for the x0 / write-first bypass that the tool pushed behind the RAM.
  (2) cpu/u_mem/reg_q.ctrl.mem_to_reg (fanout 32, 2.53 ns of route) -> u_wb wb_w_data 2:1 mux ->
      EX rs1 fwd mux -> branch compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl reset (21.023 ns).
      The WB data mux (mem_to_reg ? read_data : alu_result) sits in front of every MEM/WB->EX
      forward even though both of its inputs are known at the end of the MEM stage.
Earlier attempts (r3s0 AGU split, r3s1 ALU restructure) cut only the tail of family (1) and were
capped by the sibling family; this cuts the shared *head* of both families, which the lessons
say is the only thing left (regfile -> forward mux front, WB -> forward front).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two coupled micro-changes, no cycle-count change (same cycles, same stalls, same RVFI values):

1. Pre-muxed write-back data (mem_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv, wb_stage.sv, core.sv). Replace the
   MEM/WB `alu_result` + `read_data` pair by one `wb_data` flop loaded in the MEM stage with
   `ctrl.mem_to_reg ? load_data : in.alu_result` (the select comes from EX/MEM flops, so it adds
   one LUT level after the dmem BSRAM DO -> byte/half extract path, which has >5 ns of slack).
   wb_stage then just forwards `in.wb_data` (w_data) with no mux; the forward source into EX and the
   regfile write data come straight from 32 flops, removing one LUT level and the fanout-32
   mem_to_reg select net from family (2) and from the wb->alu_a->adder->dmem-address path.
   hold_wb behaviour is unchanged (valid cleared, data fields retained for forwarding).

2. Fabric-flop regfile (reg_file.sv). Stop Gowin from turning `regs` into a BSRAM with the ID/EX
   rs?_val flops merged into its output: tag the array with the synthesis attribute
   `(* syn_ramstyle = "registers" *)` and write the read ports as an explicit
   per-register AND-OR / case mux so no RAM is inferred (also drop the redundant
   `rs_addr == 0` clause: regs[0] is reset to 0 and never written, but keep the write-first
   bypass qualified by `w_addr != 0` so a retiring `addi x0` cannot leak into the read).
   The ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val registers (id_stage.sv, unchanged RTL) then stay ordinary fabric
   flops (tC2Q 0.23 ns) and the bypass mux runs in ID, where the path is short because the
   instruction address comes from imem_data flops (regfile 32:1 mux + bypass is ~6 LUT levels
   in a stage with ~9 ns of slack). EX sees rs1_val straight from flops: flop -> 4:1 operand AND-OR

title: Move the register file out of Gowin BSRAM into fabric flops so ID/EX operands start at fabric tC2Q
motivation:
Every recent champion's worst path starts at `cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s` (the
register file inferred as a sync-read Gowin BSRAM whose read-address/DO acts
as the ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val register; tC2Q ~2.26 ns, vs ~0.5 ns for a fabric
flop) and ends either at the dmem BSRAM address (ID/EX -> fwd mux -> ALU ->
result_sel) or at the pc flops (fwd mux -> compare/JALR add -> redirect -> pc).
Both near-critical cones (~21 ns arrival, 14 logic cells) share that BSRAM
front, so the ~1.7 ns BSRAM-vs-flop clock-to-output penalty sits directly on
the Fmax-limiting path, while all other operand sources (imm, pc, EX/MEM and
MEM/WB forward flops) are already fabric flops. Prior rounds attacked the
forward-mux/ALU/endpoint logic and gained only ~4-6% each (inside the P&R seed
spread); nobody has touched the storage macro that launches the path.

title: 2-entry BTB-directed run-ahead fetch queue verified against the head pc, redirect fanout kept to pc/flush_id/2 valid flops
motivation:
I replayed the CoreMark retirement trace (2.937M retired instrs, from the Verilator cosim) against
models of the BTB. Branch/target/return prediction is exhausted for this bar: with the champion
16-entry BTB 100K instrs mispredict (2.3% of 4.44M cycles, 1 bubble each); a 64-entry 2-bit-hysteresis
BTB gets 82K, a 16K-entry hysteresis BTB 76K, and adding a perfect RAS 62K, i.e. <= 0.9% of cycles.
So no direction/target/RAS/hysteresis/size change can pass the 4.6% bar (my first draft of this
hypothesis, 2-bit counters + 32 entries, was rejected by this measurement: +0.3% at best).
The remaining big loss is that the pc is HELD on every backend stall (dmem stall, load-use, MUL),
throwing away fetch slots while the 22% imem-stall tax is paid again after the stall. A cycle-level
pipeline model (random 22% imem/dmem stalls, 1-bubble redirect, load-use, 2-cycle MUL) calibrates to
4.452M cycles for the champion (actual 4.442M) and predicts, for a fetch queue of depth D in front of
ID: D=1 4.201M (-5.6%), D=2 4.133M (-7.2%), D=4 4.110M (-7.7%), D=8 4.107M (-7.8%). r4s2 built the D=4
version: cycles 4.086M as predicted, but Fmax fell 66.7 -> 57.1 MHz (worst path regfile -> EX ->
pc, 43 cells) because it added pred_next to ID/EX, a redir_done flop that gates the late redirect, and
4-entry pointer muxes. Depth 2 gets ~94% of the cycle win with half the storage and a shift-register
(no pointer muxes), so the cycle benefit survives if the redirect path stays exactly as shallow as
in the champion.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 2-entry shift-register fetch queue Q0/Q1 = {pc[31:2], instr} plus valid flops qv0/qv1 in
if_stage; pc (= imem_addr, BTB lookup and next_pc = btb_hit ? pred_pc : pc+4 all unchanged, flop-only)
becomes a pure fetch pointer that no longer freezes on backend stalls.
* ID view: head = qv0 ? Q0 : (imem_ready ? {pc, imem_data} : bubble/NOP, valid=0). out.pc_plus4 = head
  pc + 4 (small incrementer on the head pc; pc+4 for next_pc stays on the pc register).
* Fetch advance (no redirect): adv = imem_ready && (!qv1 || !stall_id). If the fetched instruction is
  not consumed by ID this cycle (stall_id, or queue head ahead of it) it is pushed into the first free
  slot; if consumed via the bypass it is not stored. stall_id (dmem_stall | load_use | md_stall) is
  taken from hazard_unit exactly as today and no longer includes imem_stall; the old stall_if/flush_if
  pc-hold disappears.
* Redirect (EX, late): pc <= redirect_target, qv0 <= 0, qv1 <= 0, and the existing flush_id. Nothing
  else depends on `redirect` -- in particular NO pred_next field in ID/EX and NO redir_done flop.
* Verification (the fix versus r4s2): ex_stage keeps comparing the architectural next PC with
  "the address that follows the instruction in EX", which is now fetch_pc = qv0 ? Q0.pc : pc (a flop
  mux feeding the 30-bit eq_tgt/eq_ft compares, which run in parallel with the late branch_cond chain).
  After a redirect the queue is empty and pc == target, so a held (stalled) mispredicted instruction
  redirects only once exactly as in the champion, and JALR keeps its always-redirect rule.
* Correctness invariants preserved: wrong-path instructions in the queue are dropped by the same
  redirect that fires today; a held ID instruction stays in Q0 (or is pushed from the bypass) rather
  than being re-fetched; rvfi_order, trap and pc_next semantics are untouched since all ID/EX fields
  (pc, pc_plus4, instr, valid) keep their meaning. Expect ~-7% cycles (4.44M -> ~4.13M, +7.5% iter/cycle)
  for ~+130 flops and ~+60 LUTs (Q0/Q1 pc+instr = 124 flops, 2 valid flops, head incrementer). The
  EX/regfile -> dmem-address critical path (21 ns) is untouched; the only new logic on the instr path
  is one 2:1 mux (Q0.instr vs imem_data) ahead of decode/load-use, and the stall_id -> adv -> pc-CE
  path is the same depth class as today's stall_if -> pc-CE. If Fmax drops more than ~3%, the fallback
  is depth 1 (model: -5.6% cycles, a single Q0 register with no shift).

Q0.pc : pc` feeding EX's `eq_tgt`/`eq_ft`) scored 151.93 vs the 150.95 champion, only about a tenth of the ~7% cycle win the replay model predicts, below the 4.6% bar and inside the ~6% P&R seed spread, even though it dropped r4s2's `pred_next`/`redir_done`/pointer muxes (r4s2's depth-4 build hit the predicted 4.086M cycles but fell 66.7 -> 57.1 MHz for -3.05%); the cycle win is real but Fmax gave it back at both depths (no cycles/Fmax split was recorded here, so the ~6% loss is inferred), most likely because the stall_id -> adv -> pc/Q-enable fanout, head/bypass mux and fetch_pc mux add depth to the EX compare -> redirect cone that r5s0 found is the next worst path once the regfile is fabric flops, so only retry a fetch queue (depth 1 included) against a fresh post-regfile worst-path report and keep the verify compare off any queue mux.

title: Shrink the redirect->flush_id fanout: flush-clear only the side-effecting ID/EX bits
motivation:
The champion's worst path (18.25 ns, 23 cells) is MEM/WB.mem_to_reg -> WB mux ->
EX forward mux -> branch compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX
`reg_q.ctrl.alu_op_0` (endpoint in u_id). The late `redirect` therefore fans out
through `flush_id` to every ID/EX ctrl flop (~25 flops: valid + the whole ctrl_t),
each of which has the flush term in its D/CE cone. But a flushed ID/EX slot only
needs the bits that have side effects without a `valid` qualifier downstream
to be zero: reg_write (ID fwd precompute, wb), mem_read / mem_write (dmem ports,
load-use, dmem stall), plus valid. alu_op, alu_src, branch_op, is_lui, is_auipc,
mem_width, mem_sext, mem_to_reg, is_illegal, is_branch and is_jump are only ever
consumed in EX/MEM/WB behind valid / reg_write / mem_op (redirect is
`in.valid`-qualified; md_op is `in.valid`-qualified; btb_ok needs ex_mem.valid;
rvfi is gated by valid). Clearing them on flush is dead work that only adds
fanout and a LUT input to the latest-arriving signal in the design.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
In id_stage.sv, split the ID/EX ctrl register update in two groups. Group A
(valid, reg_write, mem_read, mem_write) keeps the current flush-clear. Group B
(every other ctrl_t field: alu_op, alu_src, branch_op, is_branch, is_jump,
is_jalr, is_lui, is_auipc, mem_width, mem_sext, mem_to_reg, is_illegal) is
a plain CE flop, D = ctrl_decoded.<f>, enable = !stall, with NO flush term (the
group already captures decoded data on a flush cycle; the instruction is dead
because valid=0 and group A is zero). `flush_id` then drives ~4 flops instead of
~25, the redirect -> flush_id -> flop route loses most of its fanout-driven
routing delay and the group-B D cones drop the late input entirely (they become
a pure decode -> CE flop path as for the data fields, which the lessons already
show works: data fields are plain CE flops). The flush-free is verified
against every ID/EX ctrl consumer: ex_stage (valid-qualified redirect, md_op,
misalign_fault only changes ctrl_with_trap of a bubble), id_stage forward
precompute (reg_write cleared), hazard_unit load-use (mem_read cleared),
mem_stage / dmem ports (mem_read / mem_write cleared, so mem_misalign is 0 for a
bubble), btb training (ex_mem.valid). Bubble is_jump / is_branch may still
mux jump-vs-ALU into EX/MEM.alu_result for a dead slot; nothing reads it
(reg_write=0, valid=0). Pure micro-opt: bit-identical cycles, no new state, ~0 area.

precomputing `flush_nodstall = redirect-independent part (load_use && !dmem_stall
&& !md_stall)` so only one LUT remains between `redirect` and the flop D pin.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r6s0 (regression, -6.71%): Cutting the `redirect` -> `flush_id` sink fanout from ~25 ID/EX flops to 4 (only valid/reg_write/mem_read/mem_write keep the flush clear, the other ctrl_t fields become plain `!stall` CE flops) and refactoring `flush_id` in hazard_unit so `redirect` enters one final LUT scored 168.36 vs the 180.46 champion at supposedly identical cycles, so the ~6% P&R seed spread alone could explain the loss and there is no sign that the sink side was the lever (no cycles/Fmax split or post-change worst-path report was recorded, so this is inferred); the 18.25 ns / 23-cell path is depth-bound upstream (MEM/WB -> forward mux -> branch compare -> `redirect`), and a flush term on a flop is probably absorbed into its sync-reset/CE pins and costs little, so stop trimming flush/ctrl-clear fanout and instead cut LUT levels in the EX forward -> compare -> `redirect` cone itself, which r5s0/r5s1 already flagged as the next worst path.

title: Late (MEM-stage) redirect: register the EX branch-verify result and apply pc/flush from EX/MEM flops
motivation:
After the regfile moved to fabric flops (r5s1, 180.46) the worst paths are
the same cone in both recorded reports: MEM/WB flop -> wb mux -> EX forward
mux -> 32-bit branch-compare carry chain -> redirect -> {pc flop (r5s0:
17.96 ns, 39 cells) | flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl flops (r5s1: 18.25 ns, 23
cells)}. Two endpoints sit within ~0.3 ns of each other, so cutting only one
of them (e.g. flush_id, or a duplicated register) is capped by the sibling
(cf. r3s0). Every previous attempt tuned logic *inside* that cone (r2s0
redirect off IF/ID, r4s0 registered forward selects, r5s1 regfile); nobody
has cut the cone itself by registering the verify result. The EX compare
fan-out (pc mux 32 bits + flush of ~25 ctrl flops + hazard gating) is
dominated by wires and two to three LUT levels after branch_cond.

After the regfile moved to fabric flops (r5s1, 180.46) the worst paths are
the same cone in both recorded reports: MEM/WB flop -> wb mux -> EX forward
mux -> 32-bit branch-compare carry chain -> redirect -> {pc flop (r5s0:
17.96 ns, 39 cells) | flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl flops (r5s1: 18.25 ns, 23
cells)}. Two endpoints sit within ~0.3 ns of each other, so cutting only one
of them (e.g. flush_id, or a duplicated register) is capped by the sibling

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move the redirect *application point* from EX to MEM. EX still does the
full next-PC verify (eq_tgt / eq_ft / branch_cond -> redirect, plus
actual_next), but instead of driving the pc mux and flush_id it only
writes one new EX/MEM flop `redir` (the mispredict flag; the target is the
already-registered `ex_mem.pc_next`). The cone becomes
wb mux -> fwd mux -> compare -> redirect -> ONE flop D, with fan-out 1.

Next cycle (instruction J in MEM with ex_mem.redir=1, wrong-path J+1 in EX,
wrong-path J+2 in ID) the registered signal `redir_go = ex_mem.redir &&
!dmem_stall` (flop AND input-pin ready, shallow) drives:
  * if_stage: pc <= ex_mem.pc_next (overrides stall, exactly the way the
    EX redirect did);
  * hazard_unit: flush_id = (load_use || redir_go) && !dmem_stall &&
    !md_stall -> kills J+2 in ID;
  * ex_stage: `ex_valid = in.valid && !ex_mem.redir` replaces in.valid in
    redirect/md_op/reg_q.valid, and the EX/MEM capture becomes a bubble
    (valid=0, ctrl=0, redir=0) when ex_mem.redir is set, so J+1 never
    reaches MEM and never trains the BTB, writes memory or starts a
    MUL/DIV. md_stall can therefore never coincide with redir_go.
The redir bit is part of the EX/MEM payload: it is held under dmem_stall
(J is a BTB false-hit load/store in the only case where it also stalls)
and the redirect is applied on the first non-stalled cycle; a bubble clears
it (md_stall arm). Fetch keeps running speculatively for one extra cycle
(pc advances to A_{J+2}, J+1 is captured), which is harmless because both
are killed. JALR/mispredicted branches therefore cost 2 bubbles instead of
1, but EX-resolve -> pc/flush no longer shares a cycle with the 32-bit
compare chain. BTB training already comes from EX/MEM so it is unchanged;
rvfi_order/pc_wdata are unaffected because pc_next is still the
architectural next PC and wrong-path instructions never become valid.

Expected effect: worst-path endpoint moves from pc/ID-EX-ctrl (2-3 LUT
levels + wide fan-out after the carry chain) to a single-flop endpoint, so
Fmax is then bounded by the sibling cones (ALU adder -> EX/MEM.alu_result,
dmem load align), which earlier reports put ~1.5-2.5 ns behind (~+8-13%
Fmax). Cycle cost: +1 bubble per EX redirect; with the 16-entry BTB the
redirect rate is a few percent of instructions, i.e. ~2-4% more cycles
(4.42M -> ~4.5-4.6M). Net ~+5%. The extra state is ~2 flops plus a few
AND terms, negligible area (LUT4 3784 of 10000).

Replace `redirect`/`redirect_target` inputs by the registered redir_go / ex_mem.pc_next: pc <= redirect_target_q when redir_go (still has priority over stall).
flush_id = (load_use_hazard || redir_go) && !dmem_stall && !md_stall, with redir_go = ex_mem.redir && !dmem_stall coming from the EX/MEM register; compare cone no longer feeds it.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r6s1 (regression, +3.00%): Registering the EX next-PC verify into a new EX/MEM `redir` flop and applying `pc <= ex_mem.pc_next` / `flush_id` from MEM (`redir_go`, 2 bubbles per mispredict, wrong-path instruction in EX gated out by `ex_valid = in.valid && !ex_mem.redir` so it cannot redirect, start MUL/DIV or enter MEM) scored 185.88 vs the 180.46 champion, about half the +6% estimate and inside the ~6% P&R seed spread, so ending the forward -> compare -> `redirect` cone in a fan-out-1 flop buys little net; no cycles/Fmax split or post-change worst-path report was recorded, so the cause is inferred (the extra bubble on every JALR/BTB-miss EX redirect plausibly gives back part of the Fmax gain while the sibling ALU adder -> EX/MEM.alu_result and dmem load-align cones sit only ~1-2 ns behind), and together with r2s0/r6s0 this suggests the redirect endpoint/fan-out lever is spent, so take the next target from a fresh post-change worst-path report rather than another redirect-timing variant.

title: Registered BTB-mispredict recovery: EX verify result goes into a flop, pc/flush applied from flops one cycle later
motivation:
The champion's worst path (18.253 ns, 23 cells, 14 levels) is
MEM/WB flop -> wb mux -> EX fwd mux -> branch/target compare -> `redirect` ->
hazard `flush_id` -> ID/EX ctrl flops (the same `redirect` also drives the 32-bit
pc mux). r5s0/r5s1 removed the regfile/BSRAM front, and the lessons say the
next headroom is exactly this EX compare -> redirect cone. `redirect` is
the only late EX signal with a wide fanout (pc mux + ~25 valid/ctrl flops
+ flush gating), so its tail (redirect -> flush_id AND/OR -> CE/reset ->
flops, pc mux) is pure routing/fanout depth added after the compare chain.
The BTB already removes ~63% of redirects (cycles 4.68M -> 4.42M), so a
mispredict is now the rare event; paying one extra bubble for it (est.
~150k extra cycles, ~+3.4% of 4.42M) is cheap compared with taking the
fanout tail out of the timed cone. The other EX endpoints
(fwd -> ALU -> EX/MEM.alu_result, compare -> actual_next -> EX/MEM.pc_next,
jalr adder -> EX/MEM.pc_next) all end in a single flop with no fanout, so
once `redirect` ends in a flop the cone should be bounded by those
(a few ns shorter).

pc mux). r5s0/r5s1 removed the regfile/BSRAM front, and the lessons say the
