hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the 64-entry direct-mapped BTB array, training, 2-bit hysteresis, JALR last-target and the EX
verify / registered late redirect byte-for-byte unchanged. Change only how if_stage READS it:

1. Add a small "current entry" register set that always holds the BTB entry for the pc now being
   fetched: cur_valid, cur_ctr1 (ctr[1] only), cur_tag[5:0], cur_tgt[17:0] (~26 flops).
2. btb_hit = cur_valid && cur_ctr1 && (cur_tag == pc[13:8]) and pred_pc = {pc[31:20], cur_tgt, 2'b00}
   - a 2-level function of flops only; no pc-indexed 64:1 mux remains between the pc flops and
   next_pc.
3. Next-entry pre-read (runs in parallel with hit, ends in the cur_* flops):
     A = array[(pc[7:2] + 6'd1)]          // sequential successor (pc+4 index; 6-bit wrap, which is
                                          //   exactly idx(pc+4) because the BTB index is pc[7:2])
     B = array[cur_tgt[5:0]]              // predicted-taken successor: index = target[7:2], read
                                          //   straight from the cur_tgt flops (no dependence on hit)
     cur_next = btb_hit ? B : A,  cur_valid_next = 1
   Both reads are 64:1 muxes whose index comes from flops, so the path is flop -> (6-bit +1 for A) ->
   64:1 mux -> 2:1 (hit) -> cur flops, ~5 levels versus ~7 today, and the pc flop sees only
   cur flops -> 2 LUT levels (hit) -> next_pc 2:1 -> pc.
4. cur_* update enable = !redirect && !stall (the same CE as the pc flops; stall_if is the existing
   net - if its fan-out grows the critical stall -> pc path, duplicate the stall OR-term for the cur
   CE in hazard_unit/if_stage rather than loading the original). On redirect: cur_valid <= 0 (the
   first fetch after a late redirect is simply not predicted taken; the EX verify still checks it, so
   this only costs a possible extra redirect when the redirect target is itself a taken-predicted
   branch, modeled as <~0.2% of cycles). Optional follow-up if the cosim cycle count regresses by
   >0.3%: a third pre-read C = array[redirect_target[7:2]] from the EX/MEM.pc_next flops loaded on redirect.
5. Staleness is harmless: a training write (from EX/MEM) to an entry that cur_* already copied is not
   reflected until the next pre-read, so a prediction may be slightly stale or missed, but every
   prediction is already verified in EX against the architectural next PC, so correctness never
   depends on it. The training path still reads/updates the array's own tag/ctr (not cur_*) so
   hysteresis semantics are unchanged. `redirect`, `stall`, `flush`, imem_addr = pc and the
   if_id_t outputs keep their current logic and timing.

Expected effect: cycles ~unchanged (+<=0.2% from the unpredicted first fetch after redirect and
stale-entry windows); Fmax up because the fetch cone loses the pc -> index -> 64:1 mux -> tag compare
levels, adding ~26 flops plus ~one extra 25-bit 64:1 mux set (~500 LUT4, inside the 10000 budget).
This is a pure "remove logic from the fetch cone" predictor change, not new prediction state, so it
avoids the r9s2/r2s2 failure mode (new history/predecode state in the fetch cone). Main risks (stated
honestly): (a) the champion's critical path is the EX ALU -> ex_result -> ID bypass carry loop, so
this only moves Fmax if the fetch/stall cone is within ~1 ns of it; (b) cur_* CE fan-out on the late
stall_if net; (c) +500 LUTs of mux area may add placement/routing spread of a few percent.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r12s2 (regression, -3.99%): A look-ahead BTB read (26 `cur_en`/`cur_tag`/`cur_tgt` flops holding the entry for the pc being fetched, so `btb_hit` is `cur_en && cur_tag == pc[13:8]` and the pc flops never see the 64:1 array mux; the next entry is pre-read as `btb_hit ? array[cur_tgt[5:0]] : array[pc[7:2]+1]` with a `!stall` CE and `cur_en` cleared on redirect) scored 216.89 vs the 225.90 champion against a +4% target, inside the ~6% P&R seed spread, so taking the pc -> index -> 64:1 mux -> tag compare levels out of the fetch cone bought no measurable Fmax, which with r12s0 (deleting the imem NOP mux, zero-to-negative) says the fetch/stall cone is not the binding path on this core even though recent worst paths touched `pc`; no worst-path report or cycles/Fmax split was recorded so the cause is inferred, but the pre-read only moves the mux into the `cur_*` D cone, now with a second 25-bit 64:1 mux set, a 6-bit +1 on the A index and a `btb_hit` select fanning out to ~26 flops on top of the late `stall` CE, so do not retry fetch-cone depth reductions for Fmax unless a post-change worst-path report shows the fetch cone as the limiter.

title: Take load-use off the ID/EX data-flop clock-enable: data fields capture freely on a load-use bubble, hold only on dmem/muldiv stalls
motivation:
The champion's ID/EX register has ~230 plain data flops (pc, pc_plus4, tgt, rs1_val, rs2_val,
a_val, b_val, rd, rs?_addr, instr) whose clock-enable is `!stall_id`, with
stall_id = dmem_stall | load_use_hazard | md_stall. load_use_hazard is the only late term: it is
imem_data (BSRAM/LFSR launch) -> NOP mux -> instr[19:15]/[24:20] -> 4 five-bit compares against
ID/EX.rd and EX/MEM.rd -> AND/OR -> stall_id -> a fan-out-~230 CE net (plus the pc CE and the
flush_id clear of ~25 ctrl flops). The recent worst path of the 106.6 MHz r11s1 build was
cpu/u_if > cpu/u_id > cpu/u_if (12 cells), i.e. exactly this fetch -> ID decode/compare -> stall
-> pc/ID-EX enable family, after the ALU carry-chain loop was cleaned up. Nothing requires the
data fields to HOLD on a load-use bubble: flush_id already clears valid/ctrl (so the slot never
retires, never writes rd, never forwards, never redirects), and the consumer is re-decoded from
the unchanged IF/ID instruction the next cycle. Hold is only required for dmem_stall and md_stall
(the instruction in EX must stay put), and both of those are functions of flops only.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split id_stage's `stall` into `hold` (dmem_stall | md_stall: flop-only, early) for the data
fields and keep the full stall_id only where it is needed:
  - ID/EX data flops (pc, pc_plus4, tgt, tgt_misal, rs1_val, rs2_val, a_val, b_val, rd, rs?_addr,
    instr): `if (!hold) capture`.  On a load-use bubble they capture the (don't-care) values of the
    consumer; ctrl/valid are still cleared by flush_id, so the slot is a bubble everywhere
    (idex_wr = 0, jump_misal_ex = 0, ex_valid-gated redirect/muldiv, wb never written).
  - ID/EX ctrl/valid flops keep: flush -> clear, else !stall_id -> capture (unchanged behaviour).
  - stall_if / pc enable unchanged (still includes load_use_hazard).
hazard_unit exports a new `hold_id = dmem_stall | md_stall` (flops/ready only); core.sv routes it
to id_stage next to stall_id/flush_id. The sub-word-load invariant in id_stage's comment
(data fields HOLD while the consumer is bubbled) is relaxed: the wrong value captured on that bubble
is never consumed because ctrl/valid are cleared, and the consumer is re-captured next cycle exactly
as before. Cycle count is unchanged by construction (same bubbles, same stalls); only the
timing cone changes: the ~230 data-flop CE pins no longer see the imem_data -> load-use compare
chain, shrinking the fan-out of the late stall_id net to ~25 ctrl/valid flops + pc. Expected gain
is a few percent of Fmax if the stall cone is binding; risk is P&R noise (change is tiny).

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r13s0 (regression, +2.34%): Splitting id_stage's stall so the ~230 ID/EX data-flop clock-enables use only flop-derived `hold_id = dmem_stall | md_stall` (a load-use bubble lets pc/rs?_val/a_val/b_val/instr capture don't-care values because `flush_id` still clears valid/ctrl, so it is correct at unchanged cycles) scored 231.19 vs the 225.90 champion, under half the +5% estimate and inside the ~6% P&R seed spread, so removing the late imem_data -> load-use compare term from the data-flop CE net bought at most a couple of percent; no worst-path report was recorded so the cause is inferred, but together with r6s0 (flush fan-out cut), r12s0 (NOP-mux removal) and r12s2 (BTB look-ahead) it says the stall/flush enable cone and its fan-out are not the binding path even when the worst-path report names the `u_if -> u_id -> u_if` loop, so do not spend further rounds on stall_id/flush_id fan-out or CE-term splitting and take the next target from a fresh post-change worst-path report (this split is a safe, correct tweak that can be kept as a cheap bundle ingredient, not a lever).

title: Registered IF/ID slice with a skid entry and per-instruction pred_pc: fetch accepts on a flop-only ready (no stall_id in pc CE, no head mux in front of ID)
motivation:
Champion (r10s0) is 4.539M cycles x 102.5 MHz. Fmax is a flat wall (~14 paths within
~0.05 ns, 8-12 LUT levels, P&R spread +-6%), and every single-cone trim since r9s1 has
netted ~0 (r11s0/r11s1/r12s0/r12s1/r12s2). The one lever that has a measured, deterministic
size is cycles: four fetch-buffer attempts (r4s2 4.086M, r5s2 4.107M, r8s0 4.096M, r10s2 4.168M
vs 4.4255M at the time) removed 6-8% of cycles by letting fetch keep going while the backend
stalls (dmem stall, load-use, MUL), because today a backend stall throws away the word the
front end already fetched and re-rolls the 22% imem stall on the re-fetch. All four gave the
gain back in Fmax (-6..-15%), and they share one structure: the buffer HEAD was a mux
(`qv0 ? Q0 : imem_data`, with stall_id in its select/enable) placed in FRONT of ID, i.e.
on the regfile-read -> forward-hit -> operand-flop, load-use and tgt-adder cones, with
stall_id (load-use | dmem | md) additionally steering the pc/queue enables. No attempt has put
a plain flop between fetch and ID. A classic registered pipeline slice (IF/ID flop + skid
entry) has the same decoupling (2 entries) but ID reads only flops and the upstream "ready" is
a flop, so neither the head mux nor stall_id sits on the fetch/ID cones. The price is one extra
bubble per EX-verified redirect (~52k redirects ~ +1.1% cycles) because the redirect target is
no longer decoded in the cycle it is fetched.

predicted next PC so EX no longer needs the pc register for verification.

title: Anti-thrash BTB replacement: a tag-miss taken branch decays a hot resident entry instead of evicting it
motivation:
The remaining predictor headroom on this core is small and has to be taken
without touching the fetch cone. Cycle accounting from the log: the late
redirect costs 2 bubbles and the champion still takes ~52k EX redirects, so
ALL redirects are worth ~104k of ~4.54M cycles (~2.3%) and even a perfect
predictor cannot clear the 4.6% bar by cycles alone. Every attempt that
added state or logic to the fetch cone lost Fmax (r8s2 -4.6%, r9s2 -8.2%,
r11s2 -18.5%, r12s2 -4.0%), and r12s2 showed that removing depth from it
buys nothing either. So the only safe predictor lever is one that changes
BTB *training policy* (EX/MEM-registered inputs, per-entry write side) and
leaves the pc -> 64:1 mux -> tag compare -> next_pc lookup untouched.
The current policy is the weakest part: a taken control instruction whose
tag misses ALWAYS overwrites the resident entry (alloc ctr=2), even when the
resident is a hot, strongly-taken (ctr=3) loop branch. Two hot branches 256
bytes apart (same pc[7:2] index, different pc[13:8] tag; CoreMark's
crc/matrix/list loops and the state machine sit within a few KB) then evict
each other on every iteration and both mispredict forever.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the BTB geometry (64 entries, 6-bit tag, 18-bit target, 2-bit counter,
ctr==0 invalid, predict on tag-match && ctr>=2) and the lookup in
if_stage.sv byte-for-byte. Change only the training branch in the
per-entry always_ff:
  taken branch/JAL/JALR, tag match      : ctr saturating +1, target
                                          overwritten (unchanged).
  taken branch/JAL/JALR, tag MISS:
      resident ctr <= 1 (invalid / weak) : replace (tag, target, ctr=2)   [as today]
      resident ctr >= 2 (hot)            : do NOT replace; ctr <= ctr-1,
                                           tag/target kept. A newcomer needs
                                           to miss until the resident has
                                           decayed to 1 (1 miss from ctr=2,
                                           2 from ctr=3), after which it
                                           allocates. A resident that keeps
                                           being hit is refreshed by its own
                                           taken instances (+1) and survives.
  not-taken branch, tag match           : ctr saturating -1 (unchanged).
Because the policy only reads the entry's own ctr (already read for the
update) and the EX/MEM-registered btb_train_en / tag_eq, the write-enable of
the tag/target flops changes from `sel && btb_train_en` to
`sel && btb_train_en && (tag_eq || ctr_i < 2)`, one extra term in a
flop-to-flop cone that starts at EX/MEM flops. Nothing is added to the
fetch-side cone (pc flops -> BTB read -> next_pc -> pc), there are no new
flops, and ex_stage / hazard_unit / id_stage are untouched; correctness is
unaffected because every prediction is still verified in EX against the
architectural next PC (a stale/aliased entry only costs cycles).
Expectation, stated honestly: the effect is bounded by the ~2.3% redirect
ceiling and by how many of the 52k redirects are index-conflict evictions
(probably a minority next to the data-dependent crc/state-machine branches),
so this is a ~+1% cycle gain at neutral Fmax, i.e. below the 4.6% accept bar
by itself; it is proposed as the one predictor change whose downside is
bounded (training side only) rather than another fetch-cone edit. Success
criterion: cycles drop below 4.5389M with Fmax inside the P&R seed spread;
if cycles do not move, the thrash hypothesis is falsified and conflict
misses are not where the remaining redirects are.

Lookup, pc mux and BTB geometry unchanged.

title: Late-term diet: registered one-hot ALU legs, flop-only ID/EX data-CE, and raw-instr load-use on the pc enable
motivation:
Champion r10s0 is 4.539M cycles x 102.5 MHz. Its worst paths are a flat wall:
the 37-cell EX family (a_val/b_val -> 32-bit carry chain -> 19-way alu_op
case mux -> alt/result_sel -> ID bypass or pc_next flop, 12 levels) and the
fetch family (imem_ready / pc -> NOP mux -> load-use compare -> stall_if ->
pc CE, 9-14 cells). Two prior single-cone trims were each correct, cycle-
neutral and positive on their own, but each stayed under the 4.6% bar
because the other family immediately became the limiter:
  r11s1 (registered one-hot l_add/l_sub/l_slt/l_sltu legs, plain inferred
        carry chains): 234.84 (+3.96%); its new worst path was
        stall_gen/imem_ready -> cpu/u_if/pc_4 (fetch family, 12 cells).
  r13s0 (hold_id = dmem_stall|md_stall drives the ~230 ID/EX data-flop CE,
        load-use only bubbles valid/ctrl): 231.19 (+2.34%); its worst path
        was pc_2 -> pc_3 (fetch family, 14 cells).
The two edits touch disjoint cones (ALU result select vs stall/CE), so they
compose; the remaining late term on the fetch family is the imem_ready ->
flush_if -> instr NOP mux -> load-use compare -> stall_if -> pc-CE chain,
which can be cut with zero behavioural change (see below). This hypothesis
banks all three at once so that the EX family and the fetch family are
shortened together, which neither single-cone trim could do alone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three independent, behaviour-preserving (cycle-identical) edits, none of
which hand-rewrites an adder/compare operator (r3s1/r7s0/r11s0 lessons) and
none of which adds a consumer to the EX/MEM.redir flop or moves logic from
the D side to the Q side of a register (r8s2/r11s2 lessons):

(1) ALU legs with registered one-hot selects (r11s1 recipe). Add ctrl_t
bits l_add / l_sub / l_slt / l_sltu (decoded in decoder.sv; all other ops
remain in a small "side" case in alu.sv: AND/OR/XOR/SLL/SRL/SRA/LUI plus,
under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, the stand-in arms). alu.sv computes plain
inferred `a + b`, `a - b`, `$signed(a) < $signed(b)`, `a < b` as separate
legs and merges them with a flat AND-OR driven only by those flop selects,
so no alu_op decode sits behind the carry chains. Keep the plain `a + b`
leg shared with ex_stage's jalr_sum. Keep the merged single-sink
ex_result (do NOT export the unmerged legs into id_stage: r12s1 lost 9%
doing that). Keep ALTOPS and real arms consistent in alu.sv.

(2) Flop-only CE on the ID/EX data fields (r13s0 recipe). hazard_unit adds
hold_id = dmem_stall | md_stall (dmem_ready flop, ex_mem flop, muldiv
flops only). id_stage's data-field flops (pc, pc_plus4, tgt, tgt_misal,
rs?_val, a_val, b_val, rd, rs?_addr, instr) capture on !hold_id; ctrl/valid
keep `flush ? clear : !stall ? capture`. This is safe at identical cycles
because a load-use bubble is already killed by flush_id (valid/ctrl
cleared), so the data it captures is don't-care; the sub-word-load bypass
invariant comment in id_stage must be updated (the wrong mem_alu value may
now be captured into data fields, but the instruction is a bubble and the
consumer is re-captured next cycle exactly as before).

(3) Raw-instruction load-use for the pc enable. In hazard_unit, stall_if
currently depends on load_use_hazard computed from the NOP-muxed
if_id instr (imem_ready -> flush_if -> 32-LUT NOP mux -> rs1/rs2 field ->
four 5-bit compares -> OR -> pc CE). Because stall_if already includes
imem_stall (pc holds whenever imem_ready=0), the load-use term inside
stall_if can be computed from the raw imem_data[19:15]/[24:20] with no
change in behaviour: when imem_ready=0 stall_if is 1 either way, and when
imem_ready=1 the raw and muxed fields are identical. core.sv therefore
feeds hazard_unit a second pair of rs fields taken from io_imemData
directly for the stall_if term (stall_id / flush_id keep the muxed fields
they have today, and with (2) they no longer touch any wide CE net).
imem_ready then joins stall_if only at the final OR, one LUT level
earlier than today, which attacks exactly the imem_ready -> pc_4 path that
became r11s1's worst path.

Expected: EX family -1 to -2 levels (r11s1), fetch-family CE chain -1
level (items 2 and 3), cycles unchanged at 4,538,902. Target Fmax ~109-112
MHz (about +6..+9% vs 102.5) if the two families really are each shortened
and P&R noise (~+-3%) does not eat it; r11s1 alone showed 106.6 and r13s0
alone 104.9.

title: Word-granular direct-mapped I-cache behind a registered F stage to break the 0.78 word/cycle imem bound
motivation:
Every fetch-side attempt so far (fetch queue/skid x5, NOP-mux and look-ahead
cuts, BTB tweaks) was a decoupling change, and decoupling cannot beat the
supply bound: the random ~22% imem backpressure caps fetch at 0.78
words/cycle, so every instruction costs >= 1/0.78 = 1.28 fetch cycles however
the pipeline buffers it. Measured with the repo's own ISS on the real
CoreMark ELF (TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000, -O3): the timed region retires 2.922M
instructions, the champion spends 4.539M cycles, i.e. CPI 1.553, of which
~1.28 is the fetch bound and only ~0.27 is everything else (dmem stalls,
redirects, load-use, mul). Roughly 0.28 cycles/instruction of pure imem
backpressure is therefore the single largest removable cost, and a queue can
only hide the part that overlaps other stalls (hence +0..+2%). The only way
past the bound is to not fetch from the stalled bus: an on-chip instruction
store. CoreMark re-executes a few small kernels (list find/reverse/sort,
matrix inner loops, state machine, crc) thousands of times; the timed region
touches only 1670 unique instruction words. Offline replay of the exact
fetch stream (2.922M fetches) through a direct-mapped, 1-word-per-entry
cache gives hit rate 71.5% (64 entries), 83.3% (128), 93.8% (256), 97.0%
(512), 98.9% (1024). The bench states that stall-hiding logic is part of the
timed circuit, so this is legal and is paid for in area/Fmax, which the
structure below is designed to protect.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a tiny I-cache and make fetch hit-first, behind a registered F stage so
the cache read never lands in front of the ID cone.

1. Cache: direct-mapped, ONE WORD per entry (no line fill, no burst, no
   prefetch), 256 entries indexed by pc[9:2], tag = pc[19:10] (addresses
   are bounded below 0x100000), one valid bit per entry in a 256-flop vector
   (cleared by reset and by FENCE.I). Data (32b) and tag (10b) arrays are
   plain `logic` arrays with ONE synchronous write port and asynchronous
   read addressed directly by the pc flops, in the style of the fpga
   wrapper's dmem array; let Gowin choose LUT-RAM (~0.9k LUT4, budget is
   10k, champion 5.2k) or BSRAM. 256 entries is the knee (93.8% hits);
   512 (97.0%) if the array read is not near-critical, 128 (83.3%) if it is.
   No store snooping: without FENCE.I a stale fetch after a store to code is
   architecturally allowed (CoreMark never stores to code), and the decoder's
   already-legal FENCE/FENCE.I (opcode 0x0F, funct3==1) clears the valid
   vector. If a selftest does store to code without FENCE.I, add a
   per-store invalidate of the matching entry.
2. Hit-first fetch (IF cycle, from the pc flops): `hit = ic_valid[idx] &&
   ic_tag[idx] == pc[19:10]`; `fetch_ok = hit || io_imemReady`;
   `f_instr_d = hit ? ic_data[idx] : (io_imemReady ? io_imemData : NOP)`.
   A hit ignores imem backpressure completely. A miss the bus accepts
   (`!hit && io_imemReady`) writes {tag,data} into the entry that same cycle
   (fill-on-fetch; a fetched word is correct for its address even on a wrong
   path, so the write needs no stall_id/redirect qualification). imem_addr
   stays = pc.
3. Registered F stage (the r13s1 "registered IF/ID slice" WITHOUT the skid
   entry, which was most of its cost): F = {valid, pc, pc_plus4, pred_pc,
   instr}. F.instr/pc/pc_plus4/pred_pc capture when `!stall_id`;
   `F.valid <= fetch_ok && !redirect` and a not-ok or redirect cycle writes
   a NOP (so nothing stale with reg_write/mem_read can leak into ID/EX);
   pc advances only when `!stall_id && fetch_ok` (redirect still overrides
   everything and loads redirect_target as today). stall_id = dmem_stall |
   load_use | md_stall is all flop-derived, and load-use now compares F.instr
   flop bits instead of the imem_data input (shorter cone). The imem stall
   term leaves stall_id/flush_id/ID entirely and only gates pc CE and
   F.valid. `pred_pc` = the next_pc value loaded into pc at capture time
   (BTB prediction or pc+4); it is carried F -> ID/EX and EX's
   eq_tgt/eq_ft/eq_jalr compare against `in.pred_pc` (flop to flop) instead
   of the pc register, which is now two fetches ahead (r13s1 did exactly
   this and passed formal/cosim). The BTB lookup/training, ID bypass, EX,
   MEM, WB and muldiv are otherwise unchanged. The late redirect now costs
   3 bubbles instead of 2 (~52k redirects ~ +1.8% of the 2.92M instrs'
   cycles, ~1.1% of total); predicted-taken branches stay zero-bubble.
4. Why Fmax should hold: the array read starts at the pc flops exactly like
   the existing BTB 64:1 lookup (shown non-binding by r12s2); its outputs end
   in F flop D pins (data) or the pc/F enable (hit); imem_data -> decode /
   regfile-index paths become flop-launched; stall_id loses the imem_stall
   term; r13s1 showed the registered slice itself is Fmax-neutral (101.5 MHz
   vs 102.5) while cutting cycles 2.9%.

Expected cycle effect: with a 93.8% hit rate the fetch-limited ~0.28
CPI of imem backpressure shrinks to ~0.02 CPI on hits plus the 6% misses;
discounting the part that previously overlapped dmem/muldiv/load-use
stalls, I model ~-13..-16% total cycles (CPI 1.553 -> ~1.33) minus the
~1.1% extra redirect bubble, i.e. ~+12..+15% fitness at flat Fmax, which
still clears the +4.6% bar with up to ~8% Fmax loss.

Verification: cosim CRCs and RVFI traces are unchanged (the cache is
architecturally invisible for CoreMark). riscv-formal drives imem_data as
a per-cycle symbolic value with imemReady=1, so a hit replays an earlier
symbolic word for the same address; rvfi_insn is the instruction the core
actually executed, so insn/pc_fwd/pc_bwd/unique/liveness stay consistent
(r13s1's registered slice already passed these). Keep the ALTOPS branch
untouched.

title: Move the 64-entry BTB (ctr/tag/target) from 1664 fabric flops + 64:1 mux trees into LUT-RAM with a dual-read training copy
motivation:
Every predictor-side cycle lever on this core is spent: the late-redirect cost is 2 cycles per
EX mispredict and the whole mispredict pool is ~52k redirects (~2.3% of the 4.54M cycles), so
even a perfect predictor cannot clear the 4.6% bar on cycles (r9s2 gshare, r13s2 anti-thrash,
r12s2 look-ahead all landed -2..-8%, i.e. noise or Fmax loss). The only predictor-domain lever
left is the BTB's implementation cost. The 64x26-bit BTB (btb_ctr/btb_tag/btb_tgt in
if_stage.sv) is written as 64 generate-loop flop rows, so it is ~1664 of the 3345 FFs (50% of
the design), ~25 separate 64:1 read-mux trees (LUT4 + 4 MUX2 levels each, every pc[7:2] bit
fanning out to ~25 trees), and a 64-way write-enable decode whose CE nets fan out to ~1.7k
flops. The pc -> btb mux -> tag compare -> next_pc -> pc cone is repeatedly the reported worst
path of the best builds (r13s0: cpu/u_if pc_2 -> pc_3, 14 cells, 14.99 ns; r11s2: pc_2 -> pc_8;
r9s0: pc_2 -> pc_31; r11s1's 106.6 MHz was bound by imem_ready -> pc), and 1 ns of arrival is
worth ~10% Fmax on this core. Gowin infers distributed RAM (RAM16SDP4: async read, sync write)
from an async-read array (the early regfile rows show lutram=8), and the BTB tag/target
fields are write-only-with-no-reset by design (every prediction is verified in EX against the
architectural next PC, so arbitrary contents only cost performance). A LUT-RAM BTB replaces the
per-bit mux trees with RAM address pins driven by pc[5:2] plus a 4:1 select on pc[7:6],
deletes ~1.5k flops and ~0.5-0.7k LUTs, and removes the 64-way write decode.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rewrite only the BTB storage in if_stage.sv; the predictor policy (64 entries, index pc[7:2],
6-bit tag pc[13:8], 18-bit target [19:2], 2-bit hysteresis: allocate at 2 on tag-miss taken,
+1 on taken tag-match, -1 on not-taken tag-match, predict when ctr[1] && tag match, JALR last
target) and the interface to core.sv / ex_stage.sv stay bit-identical, so cycles are unchanged
by construction (modulo the power-on state below) and the whole effect is on area and the fetch
cone.

1. Fetch-side array: one array `logic [25:0] btb_f [0:63]` holding {ctr[1:0], tag[5:0],
   tgt[17:0]}, read combinationally at pc[7:2] (`btb_e = btb_f[pc[7:2]]`), so
   btb_hit = btb_e.ctr[1] && (btb_e.tag == pc[13:8]) and pred_pc = {pc[31:20], btb_e.tgt, 2'b00}.
   No reset on the array (see item 4). The read address is straight from the pc flops; the
   lookup is RAM16 address pins (pc[5:2]) + a 4:1 select (pc[7:6]) instead of LUT4 + 4 MUX2
   levels per bit, and pc[7:2] fan-out drops from ~25 trees each to ~28 RAM address pins and
   ~26 2-3-input muxes.
2. Training-side copy: a second, narrow array `logic [7:0] btb_t [0:63]` ({ctr, tag}) written
   with exactly the same data and enable as btb_f, read combinationally at
   widx = btb_pc[7:2] (the EX/MEM instruction's pc). It provides the old ctr/tag for the
   read-modify-write (tag_eq = (old.tag == btb_pc[13:8])), because a distributed RAM has only
   one async read address and the fetch read address is the pc. This is 2 copies x tiny
   width, i.e. ~8 extra RAM16SDP4 primitives.
3. Single write port, no per-entry decode:
      new_ctr = train_en ? (!tag_eq ? 2 : (old.ctr == 3 ? 3 : old.ctr + 1))
                         : (old.ctr - 1)                     // dec path
      wr_en   = btb_train_en || (btb_dec_en && tag_eq && old.ctr != 0)
      on wr_en: btb_f[widx] <= {new_ctr, btb_pc[13:8], tgt_or_old}; btb_t[widx] <= {new_ctr,
      btb_pc[13:8]}.
   For a decrement the tag/target are rewritten unchanged: write only the ctr/tag lanes of
   btb_f with a byte-lane style enable (separate always_ff blocks for the ctr+tag copy and the
   tgt array with wr_tgt_en = btb_train_en), so no read of the old target is needed. Training
   still comes from the registered EX/MEM signals (btb_train_en / btb_dec_en / btb_pc /
   btb_target are unchanged ports), so the late branch condition stays out of the write enable.
4. Power-on / reset: the RAM has no reset, so after `reset` the predictor keeps whatever it
   held (zero on FPGA: Gowin LUT-RAM INIT = 0 -> ctr == 0 -> invalid; zero in Verilator
   2-state; arbitrary in riscv-formal). This is correct by the existing design argument: every
   prediction is verified in EX against the architectural next PC (ex_stage eq_tgt / eq_ft /
   eq_jalr), pred_pc is always word aligned with pc[31:20] copied from the current pc (so the
   fetch address stays inside the same 1 MB window), and a garbage entry only causes one extra
   redirect. Do NOT add a reset loop (that would force flops back); if formal liveness or the
   cosim diff is unhappy with arbitrary initial contents, gate the predictor with a 1-bit
   `btb_warm` flop (reset to 0, set after the first 64 cycles by a 6-bit counter that also
   writes ctr = 0 to each entry through the single write port, hit forced low until warm).
5. Inference: write the arrays as plain `always_ff @(posedge clock) if (we) mem[wa] <= wd;`
   with combinational reads (no registered read address, no reset term, no read-during-write
   bypass). If the Gowin synthesis log (`make timing` run) shows the arrays mapped to flops or
   BSRAM instead of RAM16SDP4 (check the lutram count in the report: it should rise by ~35 and
   FF should fall by ~1500), add `(* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *)` (or the
   `/* synthesis syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram" */` comment form the Gowin frontend accepts) on
   the declarations; if it still does not infer, split into depth-16 x 4-bit sub-arrays indexed
   by pc[5:2] with the pc[7:6] select written explicitly so each maps onto one RAM16SDP4.

Why this should move fitness: (a) the pc -> BTB -> next_pc -> pc cone (a repeated worst path,
14 cells in r13s0) loses ~2 mux levels and a large fan-out, buying a chunk of the ~0.4-1 ns
that separates it from the other co-critical cones; (b) deleting ~1.5k flops (3345 -> ~1850 FF)
and their CE nets and ~0.6k LUTs shrinks the placed design by ~30% and tightens placement for
the cones that sit next to if_stage (pc, ID/EX capture, stall/flush enables); (c) it is
cycle-neutral, so unlike every earlier predictor attempt the result cannot lose on cycles.
Honest expectation: the champion's own worst path is the EX b_val -> b_val loop (15.30 ns), only
~0.3 ns behind the fetch cone, so the gain is bounded by that and by P&R seed spread (~6%);
the bet is that the area/fan-out reduction helps both. Capacity is NOT increased here (128
entries would give only ~7k fewer redirects = 0.3% of cycles for one more mux level); if the
first run shows slack in the fetch cone, the follow-up is 128 entries.

Single write port with wr_en = train_en || (dec_en && tag_eq && old_ctr != 0), saturating ctr update computed from the training-copy read, tgt array written only on train_en. lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r14s2 (regression, -0.80%): Moving the 64-entry BTB out of ~1.6k reset-free generate-loop flop rows into three `syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram"` arrays (fetch `{ctr[1],tag}` + target read async at `pc[7:2]`, a separate `{ctr,tag}` training copy read at `btb_pc[7:2]` for the read-modify-write, one write port with `wr_en = train || (dec && tag_eq && ctr != 0)`, no reset) scored 224.09 vs the 225.90 champion at cycles unchanged by construction, against a +4% estimate, so it is flat inside the ~6% P&R seed spread: halving the flop count and deleting the 64-way write decode and ~25 per-bit 64:1 read-mux trees did not move Fmax, which with r12s2 (look-ahead read, -3.99%) says the BTB array's depth, fan-out and area are not what binds this core even though `pc -> btb mux -> pc` keeps showing up in worst-path reports; no lutram/FF counts or post-change worst-path report were recorded, so whether Gowin actually inferred RAM16SDP4 (vs. leaving flops) is unverified, but do not spend further rounds on BTB storage/implementation cost (including the proposed 128-entry follow-up, which only buys ~0.3% cycles) and treat flop-count/area cuts as non-levers here until a fresh worst-path report shows the placed fetch cone, not the EX `b_val`/carry-chain loops, is the limiter.

title: One-bubble MUL fed straight from ID/EX operands (no a_lat/b_lat) plus registered one-hot ALU legs
motivation:
Champion r10s0 is 4.539M cycles x 102.5 MHz. Two measured facts from the log
frame what is left:
  (1) The ALU-cone split with registered one-hot l_add/l_sub/l_slt/l_sltu
      selects over plain Gowin-inferred carry chains (r11s1) is the only EX
      rewrite that has not lost (234.84, +3.96%, cycle-identical). It stayed
      under the 4.6% bar by itself, and the fetch/CE trims that were later
      bundled with it (r12s0, r14s0) added nothing (232.30, 225.47), so the
      extra edits in a bundle must not touch the fetch/stall cones.
  (2) Cycle-side changes are exactly additive and cannot move Fmax if they
      stay out of the late cones. The multi-cycle muldiv unit currently
      inserts TWO bubbles per MUL/MULH* (start cycle that only latches
      a_lat/b_lat, then st_mul, then done): the operands are latched into
      a_lat/b_lat although ID/EX already holds them flop-stable for the
      whole stall (ex_stage's own comment says so). CoreMark's matrix code
      (N~9: ~2*N^3 + 2*N^2 multiplies per matrix_test, plus index scaling)
      issues on the order of 1.5-2.5k MULs per iteration, so one bubble
      less per MUL is worth ~0.3-0.5% of cycles for zero added logic depth.
The two edits touch disjoint cones (EX result select vs. the muldiv
handshake / multiplier operand source), so the cycle gain stacks on the ALU
gain instead of competing with it for the same co-critical wall, and the
deletion of ~70 muldiv latch flops (a_lat, b_lat, captured flags) slightly
eases placement.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two independent, behaviour-preserving edits (no hand-rewritten adder/compare
operators, no new consumer of EX/MEM.redir, nothing moved across a register
boundary onto the fetch side):

(1) MUL starts from the ID/EX flops, not from latched copies.
    - muldiv.sv loses the a_lat/b_lat capture registers and the a_lat/b_lat
      output ports. The multiplier operands come straight from the ID/EX
      flops that ex_stage already passes in as a/b (a_val/b_val, which for
      R-type MUL/DIV equal rs1/rs2). ID/EX is held for the whole stall
      (stall_id includes md_stall and dmem_stall), so the operands are
      stable for every cycle the instruction sits in EX.
    - The multiplier sign controls must not add a decode level in front of
      the DSP: add two registered ctrl_t bits md_asgn / md_bsgn (decoded in
      decoder.sv for the R-type funct7=1 arms: asgn = !MULHU, bsgn =
      MUL|MULH, don't-care otherwise) and use mul_a = {md_asgn & a[31], a},
      mul_b = {md_bsgn & b[31], b}. The remaining op-derived flags (hi_q,
      is_div_q, want_rem_q, sdiv_q) are still captured in the idle state
      from `op` exactly as today; they are only consumed from the cycle
      after start.
    - The multiplier path stays flop -> 33x33 DSP -> prod flop, only the
      source flops change (ID/EX instead of a_lat/b_lat). prod stays
      free-running (prod <= mul_p[63:0] every cycle).
    - FSM: remove st_mul. On `start` of a MUL-class op set done <= 1
      directly (the product register is loaded at the end of the start
      cycle from the stable ID/EX operands, so it is valid in the next
      cycle). MUL-class stall drops from 2 cycles to 1 (md_stall is high
      only in the start cycle). DIV/REM keep PREP/DIV/FIX but st_prep reads
      the ID/EX operands directly (a_abs/b_abs and the qneg/rneg flags are
      computed from `a`/`b` of the held instruction instead of a_lat/b_lat);
      the DIV latency is unchanged (not on the CoreMark path).
    - consume / start / done semantics at the ex_stage boundary are
      unchanged: start = md_op && !stall (stall = dmem_stall; EX/MEM already
      holds the bubble inserted at the end of the start cycle, so no dmem
      stall can overlap done, same argument as today's st_mul -> done),
      md_stall = md_op && !done. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS the muldiv path
      stays tied off as today. The unused a_lat/b_lat outputs and the md_a /
      md_b lint scaffolding in ex_stage are deleted. test_alu.py / any
      muldiv cocotb test must be updated for the 1-cycle MUL latency and
      the new port list.
(2) Registered one-hot ALU legs (the r11s1 recipe, kept exactly flat):
    - ctrl_t gains l_add / l_sub / l_slt / l_sltu one-hot select bits decoded
      in decoder.sv from the same arms that set ALU_ADD (all ADD users:
      ADD/ADDI/LOAD/STORE/AUIPC/JALR address adds), ALU_SUB, ALU_SLT(I),
      ALU_SLTU(I). alu.sv computes plain inferred `a + b`, `a - b`,
      `$signed(a) < $signed(b)` and `a < b` as separate legs and merges
      them with one flat AND-OR driven only by those flop selects plus a
      small "side" case for AND/OR/XOR/SLL/SRL/SRA/LUI (and the ALTOPS

      plain `a + b` leg is shared with ex_stage's jalr_sum as today. No

title: LUT-RAM word I-cache with unconditional fill-on-fetch behind a registered F stage (retry of r14s1 with the BSRAM and hit->write loops removed)
motivation:
The one lever that has moved cycles by more than the P&R seed spread is the
I-cache of r14s1: it cut CoreMark cycles 4.539M -> 3.828M (-15.6%, measured
by the evaluator, CRCs and formal passed) by breaking the 0.78 word/cycle
supply bound that the random ~22% imem backpressure imposes (the timed region
retires 2.922M instructions, CPI 1.553, of which ~1.28 is pure fetch bound;
replay hit rate of a 256-entry direct-mapped word cache on the exact fetch
stream is 93.8%). It still scored only 218.03 (-3.5%) because Fmax fell to
83.5 MHz. Its recorded worst path is cpu/u_if/pc_2 -> 17 cells ->
ic_tagv_..._s (a BSRAM cell; the bench shows bsram 6 = 4 + 2, i.e. Gowin put
the cache arrays in BSRAM, not LUT-RAM). Two avoidable causes: (1) BSRAM
inference of an "async read" array merges the pc flops into the macro
address register, putting the BSRAM clk->DO (~2.3 ns) at the front of the
hit compare and then back around into the pc/F enables; (2) the fill write
was qualified by `!hit && imem_ready`, so the BSRAM read -> tag compare ->
write-enable/address loop closed through the macro. Neither is intrinsic to
the cache. Break-even is Fmax >= ~90.5 MHz at the measured 3.828M cycles
(>4.6% over 225.90); the champion runs 102.5 MHz, so there is ~12% Fmax
budget to spend on the cache. r14s2 proved this flow honours
`syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram"` (lutram 36 for the BTB, bsram unchanged).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-implement r14s1's I-cache + registered F stage with two structural
fixes that take the cache off the critical loops. Everything below is
inside if_stage / the F->ID boundary; BTB, ID bypass, EX, MEM, WB and
muldiv stay as they are.

1. Cache arrays in distributed RAM. 256 entries, direct-mapped on
   pc[9:2], full tag pc[19:10] (fetches are bounded below 0x100000).
   `ic_data [0:255]` (32b) and `ic_tag [0:255]` (10b), declared as plain
   arrays with ONE synchronous write port and an ASYNCHRONOUS read at the
   pc flops, each tagged `(* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *)` exactly
   as r14s2 did for the BTB. Acceptance check in the synth report: lutram
   jumps by ~150-200 and bsram stays at 4. If the tool still infers BSRAM,
   fall back to a generate-loop of per-entry flop rows like the BTB (LUT
   budget 10k, champion 5.2k; ~11k flops is NOT acceptable, so instead
   drop to 128 entries, hit rate 83.3%, if flops are the only option).
   The valid bits are a separate 256-flop vector `ic_valid`, cleared by
   `reset` (needed: cocotb tests reuse the sim across resets) and by a
   registered one-cycle FENCE.I pulse (decode opcode 0x0F, funct3 == 1 in
   ID, register the pulse in one flop so ID gets no 256-fanout net).
2. UNCONDITIONAL fill. `we = io_imemReady` and nothing else: write
   {pc[19:10], imem_data} into entry pc[9:2] and set ic_valid[idx], every
   cycle the bus delivers a word, hit or miss. This is correct because a
   delivered word is by definition the instruction at imem_addr, and an
   early-read (old) value is what a same-cycle hit sees. The write address,
   data and enable are all flops/inputs (pc, io_imemData, io_imemReady);
   there is no read -> compare -> write-enable loop, which was the r14s1
   worst-path endpoint. Wrong-path and stalled-pc fetches may write too;
   harmless.
3. Hit-first fetch from the pc flops: `hit = ic_valid[idx] &&
   (ic_tag[idx] == pc[19:10])`; `fetch_ok = hit || io_imemReady`;
   `f_instr_d = hit ? ic_data[idx] : (io_imemReady ? io_imemData : NOP)`.
   imem_addr stays = pc. A hit ignores imem backpressure.
4. Registered F stage (r13s1 / r14s1 structure, which passed formal and
   cosim): F = {valid, pc, pc_plus4, pred_pc, instr} flops, capture on
   `!stall_id`; `F.valid <= fetch_ok && !redirect` and a NOP is written
   when not ok or on redirect; pc advances only on `!stall_id &&
   fetch_ok` (redirect still overrides with redirect_target). `pred_pc` =
   the next_pc loaded into pc at capture time, carried F -> ID/EX and
   compared by ex_stage (eq_tgt/eq_ft/eq_jalr) instead of the fetch pc
   (pc is now two fetches ahead). imem_ready leaves stall_id / flush_id /
   the ID cone completely (it only gates pc CE and F.valid), and the
   load-use compare reads F.instr flops instead of the imem_data input, so
   the champion's worst-path family `stall_gen/imem_ready -> NOP mux ->
   regfile index -> bypass -> a_val` becomes flop-launched. The late
   redirect now squashes F, ID/EX(EX) and the fetch slot: 3 bubbles
   instead of 2 (~+1.1% cycles, already included in the measured 3.828M).
5. Why Fmax should hold. The new combinational cone in the fetch loop is
   pc flops -> RAM16 read (pc[5:2]) -> MUX2_LUT5..8 by pc[9:6] -> 10-bit
   tag compare -> `fetch_ok` -> pc CE / F.valid, i.e. the same shape and
   depth as the existing pc -> 64:1 flop mux -> tag compare -> next_pc ->
   pc BTB cone, which r12s2/r14s2 showed is not the binding path. The
   data leg ends in the 32 F.instr D pins through one LUT (hit select).
   No BSRAM macro clk->DO, no read-dependent write enable, no extra
   consumers on stall_id beyond what r13s1 already carried.

Expected: cycles ~3.83M (-15.6%, measured in r14s1 with the same F-stage
and 3-bubble redirect). Fitness = 10/3.83M x Fmax: 90.5 MHz breaks even
with +4.6%; 95 MHz = +10%; 100 MHz = +15%. If the post-change worst-path
report shows the cache read -> fetch_ok -> pc cone as binding, drop to 128
entries (replay: 83.3% hits, ~-11% cycles) before abandoning the idea.

title: Carry-free JALR last-target verify: replace jalr_sum -> 30-bit compare with an A+B==K equality network
motivation:
Cycle-side predictor headroom is spent. The 64-entry hysteresis BTB with JALR
last-target leaves ~52k EX redirects, about 2 bubbles each (~2.3% of 4.54M
cycles), and that already includes the data-dependent branches (crcu8, state
machine) no table predictor can fix. gshare (r9s2, -8%), anti-thrash
replacement (r13s2), look-ahead read (r12s2) and LUTRAM storage (r14s2) all
landed at or below noise. Any predictor change must therefore be judged on
Fmax, and the only Fmax lever left inside the predictor is the logic that
VERIFIES a prediction. In ex_stage the JALR verify is the one prediction check
that sits behind a carry chain: a_val + b_val (32-bit ALU carry chain) ->
jalr_sum[31:2] == fetch_pc[31:2] (XOR + 30-input AND tree) -> redir_c1/redir_c0
-> branch_cond mux -> EX/MEM.redir flop. The branch/JAL verifies are
flop-to-flop (tgt/pc_plus4 are ID-precomputed) and the branch case is only
chain -> 1 mux, so the JALR leg is the deepest term in the redirect cone. The
A+B==K question does not need the sum: a carry-free check is exact and has no
carry chain.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace `eq_jalr = (fetch_pc[31:2] == jalr_sum[31:2])` in ex_stage.sv with an
exact carry-free "a_val + b_val == {fetch_pc[31:2], s[1:0]}" network, built
only from flop outputs (a_val, b_val, fetch_pc):

  A = in.a_val, B = in.b_val, K = fetch_pc (bits [1:0] of the sum are not
  compared, matching the current [31:2] compare).
  n[i]   = A[i] ^ B[i] ^ K[i]               (carry-in each bit would need
                                             for sum bit i to equal K[i])
  g[i]   = (A[i] & B[i]) | ((A[i] ^ B[i]) & ~K[i])   (carry-out of bit i
                                             when sum bit i == K[i])
  c2     = carry into bit 2 from the real low 2-bit add:
           c1 = A[0]&B[0]; c2 = (A[1]&B[1]) | ((A[1]^B[1]) & c1)
  eq_jalr = (n[2] == c2) && AND_{i=2..30} (n[i+1] == g[i])

Bit 31's carry-out is ignored. This is exactly equivalent to
(A+B)[31:2] == K[31:2] for every input (it is the standard A+B=K identity),
so the redirect decision, `reg_q.redir`, and all RVFI behaviour are
unchanged; cycles are identical by construction. Each term has 6 flop-driven
inputs (2 LUT4 levels) followed by a 30-way AND (about 3 levels), roughly 5
LUT levels with no carry chain, versus carry chain + XOR + AND tree today.
The real sum `jalr_sum` is kept unchanged for `jalr_target` / `actual_next`
/ `reg_q.branch_target` (those feed flop D pins through 1-2 muxes only) and
for `jump_misal_ex` (needs only sum bit 1 = A1^B1^(A0&B0), an early chain
bit). `eq_tgt` / `eq_ft` stay as they are. No change to if_stage, BTB,
hazard_unit, id_stage or the redirect timing; nothing is added to the fetch
cone, in line with the r9s2/r11s2 lessons. Expected effect is limited to the
EX/MEM.redir endpoint family (a few percent at most, since sibling cones sit
within 1-2 ns), so this is a small, safe, zero-cycle-cost change; it is also
a clean test of whether the redirect cone, rather than the ALU -> bypass or
stall -> pc cones, is still co-critical. Keep the plain Gowin-inferred `a+b`
adder in alu.sv untouched (r3s1/r7s0/r11s0 show hand-rewriting adders and
compares loses). Verify with riscv-formal (pc_fwd / jal / jalr checks), cosim,
and a cocotb check that the new eq_jalr matches (a+b)[31:2]==pc[31:2] on
random plus carry-ripple corner vectors (all-ones + 1, 0x7fffffff + 1,
mismatch in a single high bit).
